articles.title: Bộ trưởng Bộ Xây dựng: Sẽ nâng cấp đường Hồ Chí Minh lên cao tốc
articles.text:
Cuối phiên thảo luận về kinh tế xã hội chiều 30/10, Bộ trưởng Bộ Xây dựng Trần Hồng Minh đã trao đổi, làm rõ một số vấn đề đại biểu Quốc hội nêu.
Trước vấn đề đại biểu Lý Anh Thư (đoàn An Giang) đề nghị phân định rõ việc kết thúc thực hiện đầu tư quy mô 2 làn xe với việc hoàn thành toàn bộ dự án đường Hồ Chí Minh, Bộ trưởng Bộ Xây dựng cho biết, việc hoàn thiện quy mô 2 làn xe trong năm 2026, đã khép lại giai đoạn phân kỳ dự án theo Nghị quyết 38 và Nghị quyết 66 của Quốc hội.
Mục tiêu nối thông toàn bộ tuyến đường Hồ Chí Minh từ Pác Bó (Cao Bằng) đến Đất Mũi với quy mô 2 làn xe, sau đó sẽ chuyển sang giai đoạn mới, từng bước đầu tư phù hợp với quy hoạch.
Bộ trưởng cũng khẳng định, việc kết thúc giai đoạn đầu tư quy mô 2 làn xe không có nghĩa là dự án đã hoàn thành toàn bộ, bởi theo Quy hoạch mạng lưới đường bộ thời kỳ 2021 - 2030, tầm nhìn đến năm 2050, đường Hồ Chí Minh tiếp tục là trục giao thông huyết mạch và phải đầu tư nâng cấp lên thành đường cao tốc.
Mặt khác, một dự án được coi là hoàn thành khi kết thúc tất cả các công việc thi công, đưa vào khai thác sử dụng và được cấp có thẩm quyền phê duyệt quyết toán.
Toàn tuyến đường Hồ Chí Minh dài 2.656,5 km. Đến nay đã hoàn thành 2.499 km; dự kiến đến hết tháng 12 sẽ hoàn thành 2.643 km và trong quý 1/2027 sẽ hoàn thành nốt 13 km đoạn Gò Quao - Vĩnh Thuận.
Về công tác quyết toán, giai đoạn 1 đã xong từ năm 2016; giai đoạn 2 đến nay đã hoàn thành 89% và dự kiến trong năm 2027 sẽ quyết toán hoàn thành toàn bộ giai đoạn 2.
Thông tin thêm về dự án cao tốc Rạch Giá - Hà Tiên (tuyến cao tốc CT35), Bộ trưởng Xây dựng cho biết, theo quy hoạch được duyệt, tuyến cao tốc Hà Tiên - Rạch Giá - Bạc Liêu có quy mô 4 làn xe và được đầu tư trước năm 2030.
Hiện nay, tuyến đường đang được nghiên cứu đầu tư dài 194 km, trong đó đoạn Rạch Giá - Hà Tiên dài 98 km với tổng mức đầu tư 55.000 tỷ đồng. Báo cáo đã được trình và Chính phủ đang nghiên cứu cân đối nguồn vốn.
Bộ trưởng cho biết, nếu áp dụng phương án làm cầu cạn cho đoạn tiếp theo Rạch Giá - Hà Tiên thì tổng mức đầu tư sẽ lên tới khoảng 80.000 tỷ đồng, do đó, Chính phủ cũng đang tiếp tục nghiên cứu.
Về giải pháp sử dụng cát biển, cơ quan chức năng đã xây dựng tiêu chuẩn, quy chuẩn và đưa vào sử dụng cho một số tuyến đường. Đây là nguồn cát từ cuối Sông Tiền và Sông Hậu tại Đồng bằng sông Cửu Long và khu vực khai thác đã có sẵn.
Tuy nhiên, bộ trưởng lưu ý, khi vận chuyển đến các vị trí xa kết hợp với công đoạn rửa mặn thì giá thành sản phẩm tương đối cao.
Về đề nghị đầu tư các tuyến đường sắt quốc gia, bao gồm tuyến Đông Anh - Quán Triều, tuyến Kép - Lưu Xá dài 56 km và tuyến Thái Nguyên - Tuyên Quang - Lào Cai dài 73 km, theo Bộ trưởng Xây dựng, các dự án này đã nằm trong kế hoạch sửa chữa, đầu tư trong các giai đoạn trước và sau năm 2030.
Riêng tuyến đường sắt đô thị kết nối từ Thái Nguyên về Hà Nội thuộc thẩm quyền của địa phương, ông đề nghị địa phương chủ động lập dự án và triển khai xây dựng tương tự như mô hình của Hà Nội và TP.HCM.

articles.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
articles.text:
Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- European Association for the Study of Diabetes
- Summary:
- A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
- Share:
A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.
The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).
The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.
Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous
Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.
Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.
Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.
To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.
An Intensive Diet and Exercise Program
The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.
The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.
One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).
The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.
The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.
What Participants Ate During the Study
At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.
Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.
During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).
This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).
After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.
More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission
Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).
Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.
The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.
After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.
Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.
Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.
After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.
Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects
No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.
At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.
The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.
The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.
"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."
Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters
One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.
The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.
Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.
Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.
To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.
They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."
A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes
The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.
People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.
The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.
They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.
However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.
The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

articles.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
articles.text:
Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.
- Share:
What if time is not a fundamental part of the universe, but something that emerges from the changes taking place inside it? A physicist at the University of Birmingham has created a miniature universe in the laboratory that offers a surprising new way to investigate this possibility.
Using thousands of atoms cooled to temperatures barely above absolute zero, Professor Giovanni Barontini demonstrated that the passage of time can be measured without relying on an external clock. Instead, a form of time emerges naturally from the behavior of particles within the experimental system.
The findings, published in Physical Review Research, provide experimental evidence for an intriguing idea in theoretical physics: Time may not be an essential ingredient of reality. It could arise from the relationships and changes occurring within the universe itself.
Why Some Physicists Think Time May Not Be Fundamental
We usually think of time as something that continuously moves forward, regardless of what happens around us. Seconds pass, planets orbit stars, and the universe evolves. But some theories of physics suggest that time may work very differently at the most fundamental level.
One example is the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which appears in attempts to combine quantum mechanics with gravity. In this framework, the universe can be described as a single, unchanging quantum state, with no external clock marking the passage of time. Quantum particles can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties, but the universe as a whole does not necessarily have a built-in time variable.
This creates a major puzzle. If the universe has no external clock, how can anything happen in a particular order? What determines which events come first and which happen later?
One possibility is that time emerges from the changing relationships between different parts of the universe. Barontini designed an experiment to investigate whether such a process could be observed in the laboratory.
Creating a Miniature Universe With 24,000 Atoms
To build his miniature cosmos, Barontini used a cloud of approximately 24,000 atoms cooled to just a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero. At these extraordinarily low temperatures, quantum effects become especially important, allowing researchers to study behaviors that are normally difficult to observe.
The atoms were confined inside a carefully controlled quantum system designed to remain isolated from its surroundings. Two laser beams operating at different frequencies created a thin barrier that divided the system into two regions: an observed ('bright') region and an unobserved ('dark') region.
Although the overall system was isolated from the outside world, atoms could move between these two regions.
The bright region underwent repeated cycles of expansion and contraction, resembling simplified versions of two dramatic cosmological events. The expansion was analogous to the Big Bang, while the contraction resembled a Big Crunch, a hypothetical fate of the universe in which cosmic expansion eventually reverses and everything collapses inward.
The experiment did not recreate these actual cosmic events. Instead, it provided a simplified quantum model in which researchers could investigate how a sequence of events might be reconstructed without referring to a clock outside the system.
How Time Emerged Without a Clock
The key to the experiment was entropy, a concept in physics associated with the spread or disorder (entropy) of particles and energy.
Rather than using seconds or minutes, Barontini developed a way to track time through changes in how atoms were distributed within the miniature universe.
As atoms moved between the bright and dark regions, the distribution of particles in the bright region changed. These changes provided a way to define the system's progression through time, even when the bright region alternated between expansion and contraction.
When the particle distribution increased or decreased in its spread, the system continued moving forward according to this internal measure of time. When the distribution remained unchanged, the progression of this particular form of time effectively stopped.
Importantly, this did not mean that time literally stopped in the laboratory. It meant that the internal measure of time ceased advancing when the relevant changes in the system disappeared.
Barontini called this concept "entropic time." The experiment showed that this form of time has several important properties. It moves consistently in one direction, establishing what physicists call the "arrow of time," the distinction between past and future. It also places events in the correct sequence, even as the miniature universe expands and contracts.
Perhaps most surprisingly, entropic time does not always advance at the same rate. Its progression can speed up or slow down depending on how entropy changes within the system.
A New Clue to One of Physics' Biggest Mysteries
Professor Barontini said: "In some theories of the universe, especially quantum gravity, time doesn't appear as a built-in feature. Yet in everyday life, time flows from past to future -- why is this so, when most basic laws of physics work the same way forwards and backwards?
"This study provides the first controlled experimental evidence that 'time' can be defined by changes within a system rather than as the external 'ticking clock' we think of as time. It offers new insight into the nature of time in quantum gravity that could be used to describe dynamics just as effectively as conventional time."
The distinction between everyday time and the underlying laws of physics is especially important. Many fundamental physical equations work equally well whether time is mathematically reversed or allowed to move forward. Yet our experience of the world has a clear direction: We remember the past, not the future, and events unfold in a recognizable sequence.
Entropy has long played a central role in explaining this difference. Barontini's experiment takes that connection further by demonstrating how changes in entropy can provide an operational measure of time inside a controlled quantum system.
The findings also go beyond simply arranging events in the correct order.
Barontini demonstrated that a version of the Schrödinger equation, one of the foundational equations of quantum mechanics (Schrödinger), can be expressed using entropic time. This equation describes how the quantum state of a system evolves, including changes in the probability of finding particles in particular locations or states.
In other words, the internally generated measure of time could still be used to make predictions about the quantum system's behavior, much as conventional time is used in standard quantum mechanics.
Could a Tiny Universe Help Explain the Big Bang?
For decades, questions about the origin and fundamental nature of time have largely belonged to theoretical physics, particularly quantum cosmology and quantum gravity. These fields attempt to understand how the universe behaves when quantum effects and gravity must be considered together, including under the extreme conditions associated with the early cosmos.
Barontini's experiment offers a way to investigate some of these ideas using physical systems that scientists can create, manipulate, and observe.
The miniature universe continued to obey the established equations of quantum physics while providing a different way to describe its evolution. That makes it a potentially valuable testing ground for theories in which time is not assumed to exist independently of the system being studied.
Future experiments could extend this approach to more complicated quantum systems, allowing researchers to explore models of the Big Bang and the Big Crunch in greater detail. Similar techniques might eventually help simulate aspects of black holes or distinguish between competing explanations of how time emerges.
The experiment does not establish that time is an illusion or prove that our universe lacks fundamental time. Instead, it demonstrates something that was previously difficult to test: A quantum system can possess a meaningful internal measure of time without depending on an external clock.
By creating a miniature universe from just 24,000 atoms, researchers have gained a new experimental tool for investigating a question that has challenged physicists and philosophers for centuries: What makes time flow?

Journal Reference:
- Giovanni Barontini. Testing the problem of time with cold atoms. Physical Review Research, 2026; 8 (2) DOI: 10.1103/1h9j-df4k

articles.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
articles.text:
The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.
- Share:
Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.
Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.
Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.
The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.
Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction
The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.
Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.
Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.
"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."
The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.
Ancient Crocodiles Were Far More Diverse
Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.
The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.
Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.
Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.
"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."
Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History
To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.
The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.
A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.
About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.
Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.
Two Surprising Exceptions
Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.
During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.
A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.
These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.
What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?
The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.
They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.
When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.
However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.
Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.
Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.
The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness
The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.
Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.
The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.
For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.
Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."
The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

Journal Reference:
- Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, Alexandra F. C. Howard, Grace L. Varnham, Alex Farnsworth, Paul J. Valdes, Philip D. Mannion. Climatic niche conservatism shapes the macroevolution, extinction, and survivorship of crocodile-line archosaurs. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (43) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg2217

articles.title: A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
articles.text:
A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar
- Summary:
- A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales.
- Share:
Finding the shortest route between two locations is something navigation apps like Google Maps do every day. Behind the scenes, sophisticated algorithms analyze networks of roads and intersections to identify efficient paths. But what if a computer needed to calculate the shortest distance between every possible pair of locations in an enormous network?
That challenge extends far beyond maps. Similar calculations are important for transportation systems, communication networks, and even biological structures involving proteins, neurons, or other interconnected components. As these networks grow, determining the shortest routes between all their points becomes increasingly difficult.
Computer scientists call this the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem. It involves finding the shortest distance between every pair of points in a graph. In this context, a 'graph' is simply a collection of points (called vertices) joined by connections (called edges). Those points might represent cities, PCs, subway stations, or organs, while the connections could stand for highways, cables, railway lines, or blood vessels.
Why Calculating Shortest Paths Is So Difficult
Determining the exact shortest distances across a massive network can consume enormous amounts of computing time and memory. In densely connected networks, some conventional approaches require what mathematicians call cubic time. That means doubling the number of points can increase the computational workload by roughly eight times.
Because the required computation (work) can grow much faster than the network itself, researchers have spent decades searching for more efficient methods. One promising solution is to use approximation algorithms, which calculate estimates rather than exact answers. The goal is to produce distances that are sufficiently accurate while dramatically reducing the amount of computation required.
An important advance came in 1996, when researchers Dor, Halperin, and Zwick (DHZ) developed a method capable of producing distance estimates within twice the actual shortest distance for sufficiently distant points, while operating in nearly optimal time.
This level of accuracy is known as a "2‑approximation." For example, if the shortest possible route between two locations is 10 kilometers, an estimate satisfying this guarantee would fall between 10 and 20 kilometers.
Rather than examining every possible route, the DHZ approach uses a relatively small selection of points from the network (referred to as sampled vertices). These strategically selected points serve as shortcuts that help the algorithm estimate distances more efficiently.
A Clever Shortcut With a Hidden Weakness
The approach works particularly well when the points being compared are far apart.
Consider a journey between Delhi and Chennai. Because the cities are separated by a considerable distance, the algorithm can often find a sampled point close to the shortest route. This allows it to calculate an estimate that remains within the promised limit of twice the actual distance.
However, the same strategy becomes less dependable when the two points are close together.
Imagine calculating the shortest route between two neighborhoods in the Mumbai suburbs. The sampled points might be located too far from the most direct connection, forcing the algorithm to estimate a much longer route.
For example, two points might be connected by a path containing just two edges, yet the sampled route could contain five. Because five exceeds twice the true distance of two, the result violates the "at most twice" accuracy guarantee.
This weakness meant that the original algorithm's mathematical guarantee applied only when the points were sufficiently far apart. For closer connections, the same level of accuracy could not always be assured.
That limitation remained a challenge for nearly three decades.
A New Algorithm Breaks Through a Decades-Old Limit
Now, Dr. Manoj Gupta, an Associate Professor at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, has introduced a refinement that extends the accuracy guarantee to points much closer together than earlier methods allowed.
Gupta presented his research at the 66th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 2025) in a paper titled "Improved 2-Approximate Shortest Paths for close vertex pairs."
The achievement is particularly significant because the improved algorithm preserves the overall runtime of the earlier approach while expanding the range of distances for which reliable estimates can be guaranteed.
The breakthrough comes from rethinking how points are sampled within the network.
Traditional methods depended on a collection of representative points to estimate distances. Gupta's approach instead introduces a multi-scale sampling strategy that organizes information about the network at several different levels.
By analyzing connections at multiple scales rather than relying on a single sampling layer, the algorithm can account for shorter routes that previous approaches might overlook.
This more sophisticated sampling technique reduces the minimum distance required for the 2-approximation guarantee to hold, without increasing the algorithm's overall computational complexity.
Returning to the transportation example, the original DHZ method could efficiently estimate sufficiently long journeys, such as the route between Delhi and Chennai. The improved approach extends that dependable accuracy to much shorter connections (such as Mumbai's suburbs).
The central achievement is not simply a new way to estimate distances. It is the ability to provide the same mathematical accuracy guarantee across a wider range of distances while maintaining computational efficiency.
Why This Computer Science Breakthrough Matters
Massive networks are fundamental to modern technology. Internet infrastructure, transportation systems, social media platforms, and artificial intelligence applications all depend on analyzing complicated webs of interconnected information.
In many situations, obtaining a perfectly exact distance is less important than producing a dependable estimate quickly. When networks contain enormous numbers of connections, the ability to balance accuracy and speed becomes especially valuable.
Gupta's research strengthens the mathematical foundations of algorithms designed to handle these challenges. Although the findings are theoretical and do not establish immediate improvements to specific commercial systems, they offer a better way to approach distance calculations in large networks.
The work also provides insight into how the overall structure of a network can be understood through carefully selected local connections. By improving how these relationships are sampled and analyzed, researchers can move closer to efficiently estimating distances between every pair of points in a massive system.
Progress in theoretical computer science often comes through incremental refinements rather than dramatic changes. Improving an influential result that dates back to 1996 therefore represents a meaningful advance.
By extending a longstanding accuracy guarantee without increasing overall runtime, the new algorithm pushes beyond an important mathematical boundary and strengthens the techniques underlying some of today's most complex connected systems.

articles.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
articles.text:
Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Michigan
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.
- Share:
A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.
An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.
The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.
How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog
During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.
That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.
As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.
"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."
Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.
"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."
Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars
For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.
Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.
However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.
Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.
"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.
The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.
"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.
Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.
What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies
To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.
Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.
The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.
Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.
When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.
That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.
"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.
In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.
Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization
Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.
These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.
The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.
Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.
The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.
"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."
By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.
The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.
International Research Collaboration and Funding
The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.
The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.
The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

articles.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
articles.text:
Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities.
- Share:
Not every snakebite injects venom. When venom enters the body, however, it can cause snake envenoming. This is a potentially fatal condition and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who don’t have easy access to medical care.
As researchers with decades of combined experience in snakebite and tropical disease epidemiology, we came to realise that snake envenoming faces a data crisis. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat don’t keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed.
In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from traditional healers. As a result, their cases are never captured in national health statistics.
To bridge this massive gap, we conducted a study to map the global burden of snake envenoming and related deaths.
We looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to March 31, 2025. This allowed us to update the findings from our milestone 2008 global burden study. To fill the remaining data gaps, we built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors. This allowed us to estimate envenoming and fatality rates.
We conclude from our findings that snake envenoming is a public health crisis on a far greater scale than official statistics have shown. Our results show that sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest toll.
The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability by 2030. Mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step.
Uncovering the hidden burden
To overcome the lack of reliable data, we turned to a model-based geostatistics framework.
To understand how this modelling works, think of it as predicting invisible patterns by combining known data points with environmental signals. Instead of assuming data for every region, this modelling uses statistical probability to calculate a range of likely outcomes based on environmental signals.
We fed our model with data including climate, snake species richness and socioeconomic indicators. The model then calculated the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records were completely blank.
By comparing different data sources (including hospital-reported data and regional statistics) against ground level community-survey data, our framework allowed us to account for unreported snake envenomings. It produced both a baseline floor and a potential upper ceiling for snake envenomings and fatalities.
Based on this, we estimate that at least 2.1 million people experience snake envenoming each year globally. The true number could be high as 7 million. Using our model, which adjusts for substantial under-reporting, annual deaths may range from 274,000 to 513,000.
The geographic distribution of this burden is uneven. Our research shows that sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities. That burden has likely been underestimated for decades. People in sub-Saharan Africa experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia.
Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia face a high burden, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields.
Why sub-Saharan Africa is hit hardest
The reasons sub-Saharan Africa suffers such disproportionate harm are structural rather than accidental.
Firstly, the continent hosts a rich diversity of medically important venomous species. These include saw-scaled vipers (Echis spp.), puff adders (Bitis arietans), African cobras (Naja spp.) and mambas (Dendroaspis spp.). They are responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality across the continent.
Secondly, millions of rural agricultural workers labor in open fields without protective boots and walk on unlit footpaths at night. When a bite occurs, fragile health systems, long travel distances to regional facilities and the high cost or total absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal. Similar conditions exist in parts of Asia.
We estimate that over 800,000 survivors are left with long-term physical disabilities each year, including amputations and other permanent impairments. These disabilities can reduce household income, increase healthcare costs and push already vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty.
Going forward
Meeting the World Health Organization’s goal requires moving away from guesswork and using spatial risk data to guide real-world policy.
By identifying high-risk hotspots, governments and global health partners can strategically stockpile antivenom where it is needed most, train primary healthcare workers in high-burden rural zones and improve rapid transport infrastructure.
Snake envenoming has remained hidden for too long. Better data cannot solve the problem, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.

articles.title: Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
articles.text:
Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy.
- Share:
Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.
The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.
The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]
Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.
Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions
Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]
Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.
But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.
To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.
The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.
Hidden Aggressive Cancer Cells Revealed
Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.
One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.
The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.
Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.
This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.
Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:
"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."
A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment
The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.
If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.
Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.
The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.
One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.
Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.
Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:
"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."
Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:
"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."
Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers
Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.
Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.
This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.
Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:
"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."
Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.
By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

articles.title: Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
articles.text:
Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.
- Share:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk have completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station, marking another important step in a major upgrade to the orbiting laboratory's power system. The astronauts finished their work at 3:08 p.m. EDT.
During the spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's 2A electrical power channel. This is the seventh such array added to the station, providing additional electricity for essential operations, including the station's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.
Final Spacewalk Will Complete Solar Array Upgrade
The astronauts also performed several preliminary tasks to prepare for another spacewalk scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 5. During that mission, astronauts will install the eighth and final solar array on the station's 3B power channel. NASA plans to begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with information on how to watch available through the agency.
Once the final array is installed, the International Space Station's solar power expansion will be complete. Together, the eight new arrays will increase the station's available power by as much as 30%, raising its electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
A Milestone for Space Station Operations
The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. It was also the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the assembly, maintenance, and improvement of the International Space Station.

articles.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
articles.text:
Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)
- Summary:
- Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.
- Share:
Global warming has accelerated sharply over the past decade, with Earth heating up faster than at any point since modern temperature records began in 1880. A new study from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) provides the first statistically significant evidence that the pace of global warming has increased since around 2015, even after accounting for natural factors that temporarily raise or lower global temperatures.
Researchers found that the planet has warmed at a rate of approximately 0.35°C per decade over the past 10 years, although the exact figure varies depending on the temperature dataset used. That is nearly twice the average rate of just under 0.2°C per decade recorded between 1970 and 2015. The findings suggest that global temperatures are not simply continuing to rise. The rate at which they are increasing has also become substantially faster.
"We can now demonstrate a strong and statistically significant acceleration of global warming since around 2015," says Grant Foster, a US statistics expert and co-author of the study, published in the scientific journal Geophysical Research Letters.
Scientists Uncover a Hidden Acceleration in Global Warming
Detecting changes in the underlying pace of global warming is more complicated than simply comparing temperatures from one year to the next. Natural climate patterns can temporarily make the planet warmer or cooler, potentially obscuring longer trends.
For example, El Niño can temporarily increase global temperatures by releasing heat from the tropical Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere. Volcanic eruptions can have the opposite effect when particles released into the atmosphere reflect sunlight back into space. Changes in solar activity can also influence how much energy Earth receives from the Sun.
These natural variations create fluctuations in temperature records that can make it difficult to determine whether the underlying warming trend is accelerating.
To address this problem, the researchers mathematically adjusted the temperature observations to account for these known influences. This allowed them to examine the longer warming trend more clearly, without the temporary fluctuations that can disguise changes in its pace.
"We filter out known natural influences in the observational data, so that the 'noise' is reduced, making the underlying long-term warming signal more clearly visible," Foster added.
The team analyzed five major global temperature datasets (NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT, Berkeley Earth, ERA5). These widely used records combine observations and, in some cases, additional atmospheric data to track how Earth's temperature has changed over time.
The results were remarkably consistent. Regardless of which dataset or statistical method the researchers used, they found strong evidence that global warming has accelerated.
"The adjusted data show an acceleration of global warming since 2015 with a statistical certainty of over 98 percent, consistent across all data sets examined and independent of the analysis method chosen," explains Stefan Rahmstorf, PIK researcher and lead author of the study.
In statistical terms, this means the evidence for a change in the warming trend is strong enough that the researchers could distinguish it from ordinary fluctuations in the temperature record with a confidence level exceeding 98 percent.
Even After Adjustments, 2023 and 2024 Remain the Hottest Years
One important question was whether the extraordinary global temperatures recorded in 2023 and 2024 were making the recent warming trend appear steeper than it actually was.
Both years were exceptionally hot, partly because of natural influences such as El Niño and a period of heightened solar activity known as the solar maximum. During a solar maximum, the Sun reaches the most active phase of its approximately 11-year cycle.
After accounting for these effects, the researchers found that the adjusted temperatures for 2023 and 2024 were somewhat lower than the original observations. Nevertheless, both years remained the warmest since instrumental temperature records began.
The analysis also revealed that signs of accelerating warming were already emerging in 2013 or 2014 across all five temperature datasets, indicating that the finding was not simply the result of unusually high temperatures during the most recent years.
To determine whether the warming rate had changed since the 1970s, the researchers used two different statistical techniques. The first, called quadratic trend analysis, looks for a curved pattern in temperature records that would indicate warming is speeding up rather than continuing at a constant rate.
The second, a piecewise linear model, compares warming trends across different periods and identifies when the rate of temperature increase appears to have changed. Unlike an approach that assumes the acceleration began in a particular year, this method allows the data to determine the most likely timing of the shift.
Both approaches supported the conclusion that global warming has accelerated significantly.
What Is Causing Global Warming to Accelerate?
Although the findings provide strong statistical evidence that global warming is speeding up, the study was not designed to determine exactly why the acceleration has occurred.
The researchers emphasize this distinction because detecting a change in the warming rate is different from identifying the physical processes responsible for it.
However, the observed acceleration is consistent with what current climate models can produce. These models use established physical principles to simulate how Earth's atmosphere, oceans, ice, and land respond to changes in the climate system.
The findings therefore do not suggest that climate models are fundamentally incapable of representing the recent increase in warming. Instead, they provide additional observational evidence that the pace of climate change can vary significantly over time.
Could Earth Exceed the Paris Agreement Limit Before 2030?
The acceleration has important implications for international efforts to limit global warming.
Under the Paris Agreement, countries agreed to pursue efforts to limit the long-term rise in global temperatures to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels. This threshold refers to sustained global warming rather than a single unusually hot year.
If the warming rate measured over the past decade continues, researchers warn that the planet could cross that threshold on a long-term basis sooner than previously anticipated.
"If the warming rate of the past 10 years continues, it would lead to a long-term exceedance of the 1.5°C limit of the Paris Agreement before 2030," says Stefan Rahmstorf. "How quickly the Earth continues to warm ultimately depends on how rapidly we reduce global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels to zero."
The study highlights an increasingly important concern: Earth's temperature is not only rising, but has been rising considerably faster in recent years than during the preceding decades. Whether that rapid pace continues will have major consequences for how quickly the world reaches critical climate thresholds.
