articles.title: Bằng cách nào rừng cổ đại hóa thành than, cấp nhiên liệu cho xã hội hiện đại?
articles.text:
Khi các nhà phát minh hoàn thiện hóa động cơ hơi nước, mọi ngành công nghiệp nhanh chóng chuyển đổi sang cơ chế mới. Các dây chuyền sản xuất, những con đường bộ, đường thủy và đường sắt tận dụng sức mạnh từ nước sôi để lan khắp chốn. Nhưng phải nhờ tới những vỉa than đen bóng, xã hội mới phát triển được tới tầm cao đương đại.
Thứ đá giàu carbon cũng đồng thời đẩy nhanh tốc độ biến đổi khí hậu, nhưng không vì thế mà xem nhẹ vai trò của than trong Cách mạng Công nghiệp. Tới từ Viện Smithsonian, nhà cổ sinh học Bill DiMichele khẳng định “than là vua”, và ở một số địa phương điều này vẫn đúng.
Ngay cả khi năng lượng tái tạo đã đang dần ổn định, nước Mỹ năm 2020 vẫn chứng kiến 20% sản lượng điện được tạo ra bởi các nhà máy nhiệt điện sử dụng than. “Ở thời điểm này, than vẫn rất quan trọng”, chuyên gia DiMichele khẳng định.
"Than công" không phải là một loại than cụ thể, mà định nghĩa này dùng để chỉ hiện tượng oxi hóa vật chất trong than và tạo ra màu lấp lánh. Không lâu sau khi lộ thiên, không khí sẽ oxi hóa hết vật chất gây lấp lánh.
Cũng nhờ may mắn, nhân loại có thể sinh trưởng trên cùng một thành tinh với thứ tài nguyên quý giá. Hàng trăm triệu năm trước, tại những đầm lầy rậm rạp thực vật trên những lục địa nguyên sơ, một chuỗi những hiện tượng khí hậu và vận động mảng lục địa đã giúp chôn sâu một lượng thực vật khổng lồ. Khi phương trình thêm yếu tố áp lực, nhiệt độ và thời gian, lớp thực vật biến thành than bùn, và rồi cứng lại thành than đá.
Quá trình hình thành than yêu cầu hội tụ đủ và đúng thứ tự một loạt các điều kiện. Tại sao lại có chuyện trùng hợp như vậy?
Khi các nhà địa chất học bắt đầu phân loại địa tầng, Kỷ Than đá (Carboniferous Period - kéo dài trong khoảng từ 300 tới 360 triệu năm trước) là một trong những giai đoạn được đặt tên đầu tiên. Giai đoạn này đồng thời chứng kiến thực vật sinh trưởng mạnh trên mặt đất. Từ “carboniferous”, có nghĩa “sản sinh than” trong tiếng Latin, mô tả một cách chính xác bản chất của lớp trầm tích chứa phần lớn than tại Anh Quốc.
Tuy vậy nhiều ngàn năm sau Kỷ Than đá, quá trình tạo than vẫn diễn ra tại những khu vực khác, thậm chí với quy mô còn lớn hơn. Nhà cổ thực vật vật học Kevin Boyce giải thích rằng “than không dừng [hình thành], chúng chỉ di chuyển sang những khu vực khác”. Theo dữ liệu ông có được, những vỉa than rộng lớn của Siberia, Trung Quốc và Úc đều có niên đại thuộc Kỷ Permi, giai đoạn liền sau Kỷ Than đá. Một vài thông số khảo sát cho thấy quá trình tạo thành than đá tại Kỷ Permi còn mạnh mẽ hơn kỷ “sản sinh than”.
Hình minh họa đầm lầy Kỷ Than đá.
Dù vậy, than không hình thành ở một tốc độ ổn định. Xuyên suốt lịch sử địa chất Trái đất, xen giữa những khoảng thời gian những mảng than lớn hình thành là những giai đoạn nhỏ lẻ. Tính bất đồng phát sinh câu hỏi: tại sao quá trình sinh than không nhất quán suốt bề dày lịch sử Trái đất.
Từng có một lời giải thích trong quá khứ, cho rằng Kỷ Than đá hình thành được nhiều than do cây thân gỗ vừa bắt đầu phát triển, và nấm vẫn chưa đủ hoàn thiện để phân hủy lignin, thứ polymer khiến gỗ có độ cứng như ta biết. Nhờ đó, thực vật cổ đại không biến mất mà được bảo tồn dưới nhiều lớp trầm tích, rồi biến thành than đá.
Giả định hợp lý về nhiều mặt, nhưng chưa đủ để thuyết phục toàn bộ giới chuyên gia. Đầu tiên, tỷ lệ để nấm không tổng hợp được enzyme phân hủy lignin sau hàng chục triệu năm là rất thấp. Hơn nữa, than không chỉ tới từ cây thân gỗ. Ở nhiều khu vực, phần lớn thực vật chôn vùi trong trầm tích là những cây lớn có họ hàng với thạch tùng (hay còn gọi là “thông đá”) ngày nay, vốn chứa rất ít lignin.
Trong một báo cáo khoa học xuất bản năm 2016, hai nhà nghiên cứu Boyce, DiMichele và các cộng sự phản bác giả thuyết nêu trên, đưa ra luận điểm rằng Kỷ Than đá chỉ đơn giản là hội tụ đủ những yếu tố địa chất cần có; ấy là chưa kể tới những kỷ tạo than khác.
Khắp các vùng đất, thành tố hỗ trợ việc phát sinh than hiện hữu dồi dào. Theo nhận định của ông Boyce, chỉ cần mưa nhiều (để giúp cây sinh trưởng và hình thành đầm lầy) và một hố lớn (để chứa cây) là than sẽ có thể xuất hiện theo thời gian.
Tại những đầm lầy lõng bõng nước, than bùn sẽ hình thành.
Trong Kỷ Than đá, khi các mảng lục địa xích lại gần nhau tạo nên Toàn Lục Địa (Pangaea), những va chạm giữa các mảng kiến tạo đã tạo nên những dãy núi và lòng chảo lớn. Đó chính là những hố đựng than tiềm tàng. Một số lòng chảo như vậy, có mặt tại Châu Âu ngày nay lẫn miền Đông nước Mỹ, đều xuất hiện trong điều kiện nhiệt đới nóng ẩm.
Về cơ bản, quá trình hình thành than phụ thuộc vào số lượng hố lớn nằm tại những khu vực hội tụ đủ điều kiện, cho phép vật chất hữu cơ quy tụ với số lượng lớn.
Khi thực vật chết đi tại những miền đất úng nước này, nhiều cây đổ xuống những ao tù ít hàm lượng oxy. Bởi lẽ phần lớn sinh vật có khả năng phân hủy (như vi khuẩn, nấm, v.v…) không thể sinh trưởng trong môi trường khắc nghiệt đó, thực vật không có cơ hội phân hủy. Thay vào đó, chúng mủn thành than bùn. Ngay cả vậy, than bùn cũng chưa thể trở thành than đá nếu như vùng đất khô dần và khiến than bùn tan biến. Cần một lớp trầm tích mang tính bảo quản phủ lên trên, giúp quá trình hình thành than đá bắt đầu.
Đôi khi, tại những vùng đầm lầy nằm gần biển hay những vùng cận biển nơi thường xuyên tiếp xúc với triều dâng, những hố than bùn thường hiện hữu. Hiện tượng này thường xuyên xảy ra trong các kỷ băng hà của Trái đất.
Sông băng ở Argentina.
Than bùn hình thành trong giai đoạn giá lạnh phủ khắp chốn, là khi băng cực dày lên và mực nước biển xuống thấp. Và khi băng tan, nước đưa trầm tích phủ lên hố than bùn, chôn giấu lớp thực vật mủn mà sau này sẽ trở thành than đá. Ở một số khu vực khảo cổ, những trang sử bằng đá ghi lại lớp lớp xen kẽ của trầm tích đất liền và trầm tích biển. Sâu trong đất liền, đất xói mòn cũng có thể phủ lên hố than bùn và cho kết quả tương tự.
Tiếp diễn với chu kỳ lên tới cả ngàn năm, những lớp trầm tích và than bùn mới nén lớp cũ. Khối lượng khổng lồ ép hết nước trong than bùn, để than cứng lại theo thời gian. Than nâu (lignite) dần hình thành, rồi dần biến thành than đá.
Lý do than đá xuất hiện nhiều tại Kỷ cùng tên phức tạp hơn ta tưởng, nó không chỉ là khoảng thời gian chờ cho nấm tiến hóa thêm khả năng phân hủy gỗ. Nhưng nhà nghiên cứu DiMichele lại suy nghĩ đơn giản về quá trình tự nhiên với sự góp mặt của ba yếu tố: kỷ băng hà, mưa lớn và các lớp trầm tích.
Chỉ cần lòng chảo nằm đúng chỗ, quy trình hình thành than có thể diễn ra đều đặn. “Khi bạn đã thấy hệ thống liên kết với nhau, nó chẳng còn phức tạp đến thế”, ông nói. “Các dòng sông băng đến và đi. Than bùn đồng thời hình thành và không xuất hiện. Hợp lý mà.”
Than xuất hiện ở rất nhiều nơi trên thế giới.
Bên cạnh đó, than xuất hiện ở rất nhiều nơi trên thế giới. Ngay cả ngày nay, một số vùng nhiệt đới như đảo Borneo tại Châu Á hay rừng ở Lòng chảo Congo, than bùn đang tụ thành đống với mong muốn trở thành những vỉa than đá tương lai.
Nhưng quả thực, không quy trình nào trong lịch sử hiện đại hay cận đại so sánh được với hay Kỷ Than đá và Permi. Để tạo nên những kho tàng nhiên liệu hóa thạch khổng lồ dẫn lối Cách mạng Công nghiệp, ta sẽ cần một chuỗi những sự kiện diễn ra chính xác, và không phải lúc nào Trái đất cũng sẵn.

articles.title: Cặp cá voi sát thủ giết 17 con cá mập một ngày
articles.text:
Đôi cá voi sát thủ ở ngoài khơi Nam Phi chuyên giết cá mập để moi gan trong khi bỏ lại các bộ phận khác nguyên vẹn.
Xác một con cá mập bị moi gan dạt vào bãi biển. (Ảnh: Viện hàn lâm động lực học hải dương)
Hai con cá voi sát thủ được các nhà bảo tồn hải dương đặt tên là Port và Starboard gây xáo trộn chuỗi thức ăn ở vùng biển ngoài khơi Cape Town và khiến số lượng cá mập trắng sụt giảm. Tuần trước, các nhà nghiên cứu đến từ Viện hàn lâm động lực học hải dương phát hiện tổng cộng 17 xác cá mập trong một ngày. Họ đã theo dõi thói quen săn mồi của Port và Starboard từ khi chúng xuất hiện trong khu vực vào năm 2015. Xác mỗi con cá mập đều bị xé rách và mất lá gan, cơ quan giàu dưỡng chất mà cá voi sát thủ ưa thích.
Nhóm chuyên gia cho rằng Port và Starboard chuyên ăn gan do đây là bộ phận chứa nhiều hợp chất mang tên squalene đóng vai trò quan trọng trong sản xuất hormone. Cá voi sát thủ có thể moi gan từ cá mập với độ chính xác cao. Phối hợp với nhau, đôi cá voi sát thủ dồn cá mập lên mặt nước, khiến chúng lật ngửa trước khi cắn vào bụng để lấy gan. Trừ lá gan, các cơ quan nội tạng khác trong bụng cá mập vẫn nguyên vẹn.
Cá voi sát thủ, động vật ăn thịt duy nhất săn cá mập trắng, cực kỳ thông minh và săn mồi điêu luyện. Ngoài cá mập, chúng cũng ăn cả hải cẩu, cá heo, rùa và mực. Kỹ năng săn mồi táo bạo của Port và Starboard ở Nam Phi cho phép các nhà nghiên cứu xác định cá mập có phản ứng chạy trốn. Một nghiên cứu công bố vào tháng 10/2022 chỉ ra những con cá mập lo sợ không dám quay lại môi trường đi săn tự nhiên vì chúng bị đe dọa bởi màn thảm sát của cá voi sát thủ.
"Chúng tôi lần đầu tiên quan sát phản ứng bỏ chạy của cá mập trắng trước sự hiện diện của hai con cá voi sát thủ Port và Starboard ở vịnh False vào năm 2015 và 2017. Cá mập rời bỏ môi trường sống trước đây, gây ảnh hưởng lớn tới cả hệ sinh thái và hoạt động du lịch liên quan", tiến sĩ Alison Kock, chuyên gia cá mập ở Vườn quốc gia Nam Phi, cho biết.
Các nghiên cứu trước đây ghi nhận hành vi mới lan truyền giữa những con cá voi sát thủ theo thời gian thông qua truyền bá văn hóa. Nhóm nghiên cứu hy vọng phát hiện của họ có thể giúp phát triển các biện pháp bảo tồn tốt hơn đối với cá mập trắng. Số lượng cá mập trên thế giới đã giảm hơn 70% chỉ trong 50 năm.

articles.title: Neuroscientists reveal method to train people to have lucid dreams — and it involves virtual reality and meditation
articles.text:
Neuroscientists reveal method to train people to have lucid dreams — and it involves virtual reality and meditation
People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.
Lucid dreaming — in which the dreamer is aware that they are dreaming and can sometimes influence the dream's trajectory — is a skill that can be honed, a new study finds. And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month.
The study's results could have practical benefits, said Daniel Morris, a cognitive neuroscientist at Northwestern University who studies dreams and was not involved with the work. "Lucid dreaming can benefit people with nightmares by allowing them to transform their nightmares into positive dreams and feel greater agency in their dreams," Morris told Live Science in an email.
Before this study, published Sept. 28 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, neuroscientists tried to induce lucid dreaming with various methods. These included meditation exercises and so-called reality checks, in which participants ask themselves while awake whether unusual phenomena they encounter — such as people wearing odd Halloween costumes — are real or if they're dreaming. The idea is that they will ask themselves the same question in their sleep during bizarre dreams.
However, "for most people, our day-to-day lives may not feel 'dream-like,'" Morris said, explaining why reality checks have had mixed results and don't reliably trigger lucid dreaming.
Since dream-like scenarios are rare in waking life, the neuroscientists behind the new study used VR simulations of bizarre situations to complement reality-check exercises.
The team, based at the University of Trento in Italy, recruited university students and asked them to meditate and then perform the VR training. The meditation was intended to increase students' awareness of what they were thinking about in a given moment. Each time they encountered bizarre happenings in the VR environment, such as objects or people violating laws of physics or rapid switches from one scene to another, they performed reality checks.
After the training, participants went home and were asked to keep a dream diary that they wrote in every morning. They also filled out daily questionnaires, citing the number of dreams they recalled and how many they remembered being lucid.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The participants experienced lucid dreams four times more often than participants did in a second group that did reality checks without performing any meditation or VR training. The study also included another comparison group, in which participants carried out reality checks during realistic rather than dream-like VR simulations; these participants were over eight times less likely to report lucid dreams. This latter comparison ensured that the results were not caused solely by the use of VR, the researchers said.
It was particularly surprising to find that such little training with the dream-like VR simulations was needed to develop lucid dreaming as a skill, said study co-author Nicola De Pisapia, a neuroscientist at the University of Trento. His team ran the experiment for only a month because any longer would have been too demanding for the participants, De Pisapia noted.
Study co-author Andrea Signorelli, a doctoral student in De Pisapia's lab, thinks the VR intervention is at the heart of why the approach worked. People often don't realize that they're dreaming because the dreams "fool" your senses and feel realistic in the moment, he explained.
"Virtual reality is the technology to fool you on stereoscopic vision and auditory information," he said. The term "stereoscopic" refers to techniques that create 3D illusions from 2D images by mimicking how human eyes see.
"It's basically the most immersive technology that we have at the moment," making it a good intervention for reality check exercises, Signorelli said.
The team also compared the number of lucid dreams participants reported against their total number of recalled dreams, which revealed an interesting pattern. On average, participants in each group recalled more dreams after starting the experiment than they did beforehand. However, the dream-simulating VR group recalled the fewest dreams overall after entering the experiment, even though they had the highest number of lucid dreams.
Signorelli speculated that perhaps it takes a lot of energy to have lucid dreams, which could divert resources away from recalling other dreams. Morris argued that, alternatively, participants in the lucid-dream VR group "may have been less motivated to report non-lucid dreams than the control groups." So there may have been some bias in the reporting.
Related stories
The study had some limitations, such as its small sample size of 38 participants. Plus, neither of the two control groups were asked to meditate, so it is impossible to say whether the meditations or the dreamlike VR sessions had more influence over lucid dreaming in the test group.
The team is now doing a follow-up study in which the meditation part has been removed, Signorelli said, to reveal whether the VR dream scenarios are the critical factor, as suspected.
Signorelli said that he would like to see lucid-dream training tailored for each individual. For example, the VR simulations could be personalized to simulate a recurrent nightmare that a given person experiences, training them to recognize triggers specific to that dream, he said.
"Other future research could explore the potential therapeutic benefits of this intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety, or PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]," Morris suggested.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Signorelli, A., Tormen, F., Dal Bianco, B., & De Pisapia, N. (2026). Virtual reality as a metacognitive training tool for lucid dreaming. Frontiers in Psychology, 17(1924370). https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924370

Kamal Nahas is a freelance contributor based in Oxford, U.K. His work has appeared in New Scientist, Science and The Scientist, among other outlets, and he mainly covers research on evolution, health and technology. He holds a PhD in pathology from the University of Cambridge and a master's degree in immunology from the University of Oxford. He currently works as a microscopist at the Diamond Light Source, the U.K.'s synchrotron. When he's not writing, you can find him hunting for fossils on the Jurassic Coast.

articles.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
articles.text:
Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Mayo Clinic
- Summary:
- Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.
- Share:
Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.
The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.
The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.
"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.
Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike
Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.
To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.
Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.
Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..
A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation
Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.
The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.
In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.
The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.
Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:
- "Distinct senotypes in p16- and p21-positive cells across human and mouse aging tissues"
- "Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP"
- "Mitochondrial RNA cytosolic leakage drives the SASP"
Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells
The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.
The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.
When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.
Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.
These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.
Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:
- "IL-23R is a senescence-linked circulating and tissue biomarker of aging"
- "Spatial mapping and senolytic targeting of senescent and disease-associated microglia in aged mouse brain white matter"
A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research
Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.
The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.
Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.
The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.
By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

articles.title: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune could destroy each other billions of years sooner than we thought, new simulations hint
articles.text:
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune will probably destroy each other after the sun runs out of fuel, new simulations hint
The outer solar system will descend into chaos just a few billion years after the sun exhausts its fuel — much sooner than scientists previously thought, a new study suggests.
When the sun inevitably dies, not even the outer solar system will be safe from the resulting chaos, new research hints.Scientists have long thought the outer solar system — which comprises the four giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — would mostly retain its present-day appearance for hundreds of billions of years to come. But a new study suggests that the outer giants may develop weirdly shaped orbits as the sun runs out of fuel, causing the planets to cross paths and destroy themselves through collisions within three billion years of the sun's transformation into a red giant.
The findings, published Sept. 21 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could change our understanding of what kinds of exoplanets orbit certain stars.
In about 5 billion years, the sun will balloon outward as a red giant after exhausting all of the hydrogen in its core. During this red giant phase, our star will swell to 100 times its present-day size, gobbling up Mercury, Venus and possibly even Earth in the process, Nathan Kaib, a planetary scientist at the University of Oklahoma who wasn't involved in the new research, told Live Science in an email. Following this violent swelling, the sun will crumple into a collapsed core called a white dwarf.
Until now, scientists thought the four outer planets would escape this phase relatively unscathed. A 1998 simulation-based study suggested that the gas the sun spews from its outer layers will push this planetary quartet outward, doubling the radius of each planet's orbit. Only the gravitational impact of a runaway star could destabilize this new order, and such events are thought to occur only once every billion billion years.
Solar recoil
These predictions hinged on the assumption that the sun will eject its outer layers smoothly. However, recent observations of stars suggest a jerkier loss of mass, with gas clouds lofted by plumes of plasma in the sun — as though our star were spitting out mass blobs. "They're kind of like coronal mass ejections, except much larger," Jim Fuller, a professor of theoretical astrophysics at Caltech and co-author of the new study, told Live Science in an email.
Each "blob" pushes the star backward, similar to how a fired bullet causes a gun to recoil. Although every push is small, moving the sun just a few feet per second, many pushes can, over time, impart the equivalent of an enormous kick that alters the sun's speed by several hundred feet per second. In fact, astronomers have already seen white dwarfs suffer such kicks in other star systems.
When Fuller, who studied these kicks, described them to Konstantin Batygin, a professor of planetary science at Caltech and the study's first author, Batygin "realized this would have important consequences for the evolution of our own solar system," Fuller said. That's because the kicks change the sun's gravitational pulls on everything around it.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Chaos at the edge of town
To determine how the sun's mass loss would influence the giant planets, Batygin created computer-based simulations of the sun and the outer planets. The researchers considered three scenarios: if the sun lost its mass smoothly, if it spit out distinct mass blobs during its entire time evolving as a red giant, and if the sun spewed the blobs only during its last stages. The researchers also varied each ejected blob's mass.
Related stories
The first scenario produced results similar to those of previous studies, with the outer solar system retaining almost all of its features for billions of years. In contrast, the other two cases had drastically different results. Using 672 simulations, the researchers found that if the sun lost mass in blobs, the giant planets would be thrown into chaos, switching places, developing weirdly oval-shaped orbits, and even getting ejected out of the solar system entirely. Most dramatically, in 96% of the simulations with the heaviest ejected mass packets, the planets get destroyed as they crashed into each other.
These developments also happened much more rapidly — less than a few hundred million years after the sun transformed into a white dwarf, or even during the red giant phase, in the most extreme scenarios.
The study's findings hint that analogues of the present-day outer solar system around white dwarf stars are less likely to exist than previously thought. Kaib noted that the study's results suggest that planets with oval-shaped orbits should dominate instead. It's thought that habitable planets could exist around white dwarfs, but this study's findings show that our understanding of those distant star systems may be incomplete, and that such worlds may, in reality, be unstable.
Batygin, K., Fuller, J., & Adams, F. C. (2026). Terminal instability of the solar system triggered by stochastic solar mass loss. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1009(2), L22. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea290

She did a masters degree in biology, specializing in neuroscience, from the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India, and is almost through with a bachelor's degree in archaeology from the University of Leicester, UK. She's also a self-taught space enthusiast, and so loves writing about topics in astronomy, archaeology and neuroscience.

articles.title: Phát hiện hai lỗ đen gần Trái đất nhất, thuộc loại chưa từng thấy
articles.text:
Hai lỗ đen ẩn nấp ở sân sau của Trái đất với khoảng cách chỉ 1.560 và 3.800 năm ánh sáng, đại diện cho một loại mà các nhà thiên văn học chưa từng thấy.
Các lỗ đen được đặt tên là Gaia BH1 và Gaia BH2, do được phát hiện từ dữ liệu của tàu vũ trụ Gaia do Cơ quan Vũ trụ châu Âu (ESA) điều hành.
Theo tờ Space, Gaia BH1 nằm cách Trái đất 1.560 năm ánh sáng về hướng chòm sao Xà Phu, trong khi Gaia BH2 cách Trái đất 3.800 năm ánh sáng về hướng chòm sao Bán Nhân Mã, thuộc khu vực được gọi là "sân sau của Trái đất", vùng mà hầu hết các kính thiên văn không hướng về.
Đây là các khoảng cách gần kỷ lục của các lỗ đen từng được phát hiện quanh Trái đất.
Hai lỗ đen vừa được phát hiện - (Ảnh: ESA).
Nó thuộc về một hệ sao hoàn toàn tương phản với thế giới chúng ta. Vây quanh Mặt trời là 8 hành tinh và rất nhiều thiên thể khác với nhiều cái có thể có sự sống, trong đó có một Trái Đất xanh tươi, đông đúc.
Thế nhưng, quanh một ngôi sao y hệt chúng ta trong chòm sao Xà Phu chỉ có lỗ đen nói trên, tạo thành một hệ sao nhị phân ma quái, chết chóc.
Trưởng nhóm nghiên cứu Kareem E-Badry, người đồng thời làm việc cho Trung tâm Vật lý thiên văn Harvard-Smithsonian (Mỹ) và Viện Thiên văn học Max Plack (Đức), cho biết: "Điều khiến nhóm lỗ đen mới này khác biệt là chúng có khoảng cách lớn với các ngôi sao đồng hành".
Lỗ đen khối lượng sao, tức loại lỗ đen nhỏ như Gaia BH1 và Gaia BH2 có thể đồng hành với một ngôi sao và tạo ra một hệ thống phát sáng trong bức xạ tia X trong các quan sát.
Chúng thường khá gần nhau và tương tác, trong đó lỗ đen ăn mòn dần ngôi sao đồng hành và chính điều đó khiến hệ thống phát sáng.
Tuy nhiên, hai lỗ đen này ở xa, hoàn toàn tối vì hiệu ứng hấp dẫn mà chúng tác động lên bạn đồng hành không hề giúp chúng phát sáng. Cách mà các cặp đôi xa cách kỳ lạ này vẫn chưa thể lý giải.
Các nhà khoa học hy vọng câu trả lời sẽ được tìm thấy khi có thêm những hệ thống tương tự lộ diện, một nhiệm vụ khó bởi những lỗ đen tối tăm này rất khó để quan sát - lý do chúng ở gần Trái đất như thế mà bấy lâu vẫn ẩn nấp thành công.
Vĩ đại nhất trong các loại lỗ đen là các lỗ đen quái vật (lỗ đen siêu khối) ở trung tâm các thiên hà. Ví dụ lỗ đen Sagittarius A* (Nhân Mã A*) ở trung tâm thiên hà chứa Trái đất Milky Way (Ngân Hà) có khối lượng tương đương 4 triệu Mặt trời.

articles.title: Live Science readers respond to whether AI is making them lazy
articles.text:
'It isn't under control at all': Live Science readers respond to whether AI is making them lazy
A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.
While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.
The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.
In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.
More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."
"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."
Related stories
- Can AI detect cognitive decline better than a doctor? New study reveals surprising accuracy
- Doctors say AI model can predict 'biological age' from a selfie — and want to use it to guide cancer treatment
- 'There's a sense that these algorithms are objective and they get to know you': How social media warps our understanding of healthcare
Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."
Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."
Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
articles.text:
1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
- New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
- Share:
An archaeological site in the Jordan Valley is rewriting the timeline of early human migration. New research shows that 'Ubeidiya is at least 1.9 million years old, placing humans in the region hundreds of thousands of years earlier than previously believed. The revised dating makes 'Ubeidiya, alongside Dmanisi in Georgia, one of the oldest known sites of early human activity outside Africa. The findings suggest that ancient human populations, using different types of stone tools, had already spread into the Levant during a crucial early period of human expansion beyond Africa.
The research was led by Prof. Ari Matmon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Prof. Omry Barzilai of the University of Haifa, and Prof. Miriam Belmaker of the University of Tulsa. By combining three advanced dating methods, the team established a more reliable timeline for 'Ubeidiya, a site that has played an important role in research on human evolution.
Their findings indicate that the site is at least 1.9 million years old, making it one of the earliest known locations where ancient humans lived outside their African homeland.
Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Early Human Activity
The 'Ubeidiya Formation has attracted scientific attention for decades because of its early evidence of the Acheulean stone tool tradition. This technology is known for large tools shaped on both sides, including hand axes. The site also contains a rich collection of animal fossils, representing species originally associated with Africa and Asia, including several that are now extinct.
Despite its importance, researchers have struggled to establish exactly when early humans occupied the area. Previous estimates generally placed 'Ubeidiya between 1.2 million and 1.6 million years old, but those dates relied on comparisons with other archaeological and geological evidence rather than direct measurements.
To resolve the uncertainty, the researchers collected new samples from the site and analyzed them using three complementary dating techniques. Each provided an independent source of evidence about the age of the ancient deposits.
The first technique, called cosmogenic isotope burial dating, uses rare isotopes that form when cosmic rays interact with rocks exposed at Earth's surface. After the rocks become buried, these isotopes decay at known rates. Measuring what remains allows scientists to estimate how long the rocks have been underground.
The researchers also investigated evidence of Earth's ancient magnetic field recorded in sediments deposited at the bottom of a lake. As these sediments accumulated, they preserved the orientation of the magnetic field at the time. Comparing these records with known magnetic reversals showed that the deposits formed during the Matuyama Chron, a period that began more than two million years ago.
A third technique involved fossilized shells from Melanopsis, a genus of freshwater snails found within the sediment. Using uranium-lead dating, the team was able to establish a minimum age for the geological layers containing the ancient stone tools.
Together, the three approaches pointed to a much older age than earlier estimates.
A 1.9-Million-Year-Old Discovery Changes the Human Migration Timeline
The combined evidence indicates that 'Ubeidiya dates back at least 1.9 million years, significantly changing the timeline of early human settlement beyond Africa.
This places the Jordan Valley site at approximately the same age as Dmanisi in Georgia, another major location for understanding early human migration. The similarity in age suggests that ancient human populations were expanding into different regions around the same time.
The findings also raise intriguing questions about how these early migrations unfolded. Evidence from the two sites suggests that different groups of ancient humans may have carried distinct stone tool technologies out of Africa during overlapping periods.
These included the Oldowan tradition, associated with relatively simple stone tools, and the more sophisticated Acheulean tradition, known for carefully shaped tools such as hand axes. Rather than spreading in a single technological sequence, these different approaches to toolmaking may have traveled beyond Africa at roughly the same time as separate groups of early humans entered new environments.
Solving a Three-Million-Year-Old Dating Puzzle
The researchers also had to explain an unexpected complication in their results. Initial measurements of cosmogenic isotopes suggested that some rocks were approximately three million years old, considerably older than indicated by the site's magnetic, fossil, geological, and archaeological evidence.
Further investigation revealed why the measurements appeared to conflict.
The sediments had undergone a complicated history of repeated deposition, burial, exposure, and movement within the Dead Sea rift and the surrounding landscape. Some of the material had been buried long before it was eventually transported and deposited again near the ancient lake at 'Ubeidiya.
This recycling meant that the geological history recorded by certain rocks extended much farther into the past than the formation of the archaeological layers themselves.
As the researchers explained:
"The exposure-burial history that emerges from the model implies recycling of sediments previously deposited and buried in the rift valley... and then redeposited along the 'Ubeidiya paleo lake shoreline."
By accounting for this complex sediment history, the team reconciled the conflicting measurements and strengthened the evidence for the site's revised age.
The results establish 'Ubeidiya as one of the oldest known centers of early human activity outside Africa. They also suggest that the movement of our ancient relatives into new territories was already underway 1.9 million years ago, potentially involving multiple populations with different toolmaking traditions.

articles.title: Lý do nào khiến nấm truffle siêu đắt đỏ, hầu như chỉ dành cho giới thượng lưu?
articles.text:
Truyền thuyết kể lại rằng có một người nông dân phát hiện con lợn của anh ta đào được một phần rễ cây. Sau khi ăn chiếc rễ có hình dáng như cây nấm đó, con lợn đã ngất đi. Xem xét lại, người nông dân phát hiện ra đó chính là loại củ thơm mà ngày nay chúng ta vẫn gọi là nấm truffle (nấm cục).
Truffle từ lâu đã được biết đến với nhiều nền văn hóa khác nhau, có những công thức nấu ăn được ghi chép rằng người Ai Cập cổ đại ăn nấm được bọc trong mỡ ngỗng. Người Hy Lạp và La Mã lại sử dụng chúng cho mục đích chữa bệnh.
Tuy nhiên, nấm truffle lại đã biến mất khỏi sử sách trong Thời kỳ Đen tối khi mùi thơm của chúng bị coi là “món ăn phù thủy”, và không xuất hiện trên bàn ăn của giới quý tộc cho đến thời vua Louis XIV của Pháp vào thế kỷ 17. Lúc này, nấm truffle trở lại là cái tên đầu tiên trong danh sách thực phẩm tinh tế của giới thượng lưu châu Âu.
Truffle từ lâu đã được biết đến với nhiều nền văn hóa khác nhau. (Ảnh: 8½ Otto E Mezzo Bombana)
Mặc dù lợn có liên kết với việc phát hiện ra nấm cục nhưng chúng không còn được sử dụng để thu hoạch các loại củ quý hiếm nữa.
Luca Stanzani, Phó chủ tịch của thương hiệu nấm truffle của Ý Appennino tại Mỹ cho biết: “Ở Ý, dùng lợn để săn nấm cục là bất hợp pháp vì nhiều lý do. Thứ nhất, lợn sẽ ăn nấm cục và thứ hai là chúng có xu hướng phá hoại hệ động vật tự nhiên của rừng. Thay vào đó, người ta dùng chó để săn nấm. Đó là những con chó được huấn luyện chỉ để làm việc này”.
Truffle là một loại nấm tự nhiên, mọc phía dưới lòng đất thay vì ở trên bề mặt như các loại nấm thông thường khác. Truffles còn được mệnh danh là loài nấm "kỳ quái", không có một dấu hiệu nào cho con người biết rằng nó tồn tại vì chúng ẩn sâu trong những lớp đất tối tăm. Vậy nên để tìm được truffles, người ta phải huấn luyện chó săn lần theo mùi hương và đào đất.
Nấm truffles gần như không thể trồng được, chúng chỉ có thể mọc dại ở những thổ nhưỡng nhất định trong khu vực châu Âu. Một năm có thể thu thập được bao nhiêu loại nấm này thì phải phụ thuộc vào sự ưu ái của mẹ thiên nhiên.
Dùng chó săn nấm cục là công việc thường thấy ở Ý. (Ảnh: Handout)
Có hai loại nấm cục trên thế giới là nấm trắng và nấm đen. Khác nhau về màu sắc và mùi vị của chúng cũng không giống nhau. Nấm cục trắng có mùi hơi hăng giống như hẹ tây và hương thảo. Trong khi đó, nấm cục đen có mùi vị tương đối tươi mát như là trái cây, các loại rau dạng thì là, cần tây và húng quế.
Một đầu bếp tên là Claudio Favero, người phụ trách ẩm thực tại Sabatini Ristorante Italiano cho biết nấm cục trắng hợp với món ăn có hương vị trung tính nên thường kết hợp với pho mát, khoai tây, trứng, hạt dẻ và tôm hùm.
Trong khi đó, nấm cục đen có xu hướng kém thơm hơn và có thể bị khét trong khi nấu nên thường dùng làm nước sốt vì khá hợp với thịt. Với nấm cục trắng, đầu bếp có thể bào ra bao nhiêu tùy thích lên món ăn và nó sẽ rất thơm, còn với màu đen, khi cạo được khoảng 30g thì nấm sẽ bắt đầu có vị hơi đắng.
Ngoài ra còn có một loại nấm màu đỏ tía, thường rẻ hơn các loại màu trắng và đen do hương vị nhẹ hơn. Nấm màu đỏ tía chủ yếu mọc ở Pháp và Ý và được đặc trưng bởi màu nâu sẫm đỏ không thể nhầm lẫn với những loại khác. Nó có hương vị dịu nhé, phù hợp với các món thịt quay, thịt gia cầm và thịt thú săn.
Nấm đen và đỏ tía có thể bảo quản được 1 - 2 tuần trong khi nấm trắng được khuyến cáo nên sử dụng trong vòng 5 ngày để đảm bảo mùi hương lẫn vị ngon của nấm.
Nấm cục đen. (Ảnh: GourmetFoodStore)
Vì sao truffle lại đắt đỏ?
Truffle được mệnh danh là "vua của các loại nấm". Chúng có giá trị dinh dưỡng cao, mùi hương đặc trưng không thể nhầm lẫn. Mỗi món ăn chỉ cần 1 lát nấm là đã có thể dậy lên hương vị tuyệt hảo.
Chính vì sự quý hiếm trong việc tìm kiếm và mùi vị đặc trưng không lẫn đi đâu được mà giá của loại nấm này còn đắt hơn cả tôm hùm, đắt hơn vàng miếng và bất kỳ loại nấm nào khác.
Vào mùa thu năm nay, giá nấm cục đen rơi vào khoảng 400 USD/450g trong khi nấm trắng được bán với giá gấp 10 lần - 4.000 USD. Lý do của sự chênh lệch giá này đơn giản chỉ dựa vào cung và cầu.
Nấm cục đen có thể tìm thấy ở bất cứ đâu ở châu Âu như Romania, Bulgaria và Slovenia nhưng nấm cục trắng thì chỉ có ở Ý và một số vùng nhỏ ở Serbia, nhưng chủ yếu vẫn là trên đất Ý. Điều này khiến cho việc thu hoạch nấm cục trắng hàng năm phụ thuộc vào nhiều yếu tố. Vào những tháng mùa hè, nếu trời không mưa từ tháng 5 đến tháng 8 thì nấm sẽ không thể phát triển vì đất quá khô.
Chất lượng của nấm cục trắng phụ thuộc vào thời tiết và chất lượng đất đai. Mùi hương của nấm cục trắng cũng là một yếu tố khác để quyết định giá bán. Như loại nấm cục magnatum pico nổi tiếng và độc quyền của vùng Alba nước Ý là loại tươi mát, hương thơm nồng nàn và tinh tế được coi là nguyên liệu không gì thay thế, khiến nó trở thành thành phần tuyệt vời tạo nên độ ngon miệng của một món ăn.
Nấm cục trắng. (Ảnh: Paper Moon)
Đầu bếp Umberto Bombana, người đồng sở hữu nhà hàng 8½ Otto e Mezzo Bombana và thêm nhà hàng 3 sao Michelin ở Hong Kong được mệnh danh là “vua nấm cục trắng”. Hàng năm ông đều tổ chức đấu giá nấm để ủng hộ quỹ trẻ em của địa phương. Vào năm 2019, một người Hong Kong đã trả 132.000 USD để mua viên nấm cục trắng trọng lượng 1kg. Cục nấm này sau đó được dùng trong bữa ăn 5 món có giá 1.999 USD/người.

articles.title: Nearly 30% of US adults admit to lying about or exaggerating their symptoms to get antibiotics from doctors, survey finds
articles.text:
Nearly 30% of US adults admit to lying about or exaggerating their symptoms to get antibiotics from doctors, survey finds
In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.
Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.
"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.
However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.
A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.
Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.
Motivations for lying
The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.
The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.
Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.
"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.
Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.
The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.
About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.
"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.
The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.
Doctors are still the gatekeepers
Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.
One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.
But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.
Related stories
"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."
When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.
"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

articles.title: The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure
articles.text:
The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- BMJ Group
- Summary:
- A surprisingly simple exercise routine could help lower blood pressure without requiring daily workouts or expensive equipment. In a study of 100 adults, researchers found that wall squats performed just once or twice a week helped maintain significant reductions in systolic blood pressure over the short term.
- Share:
New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.
The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.
Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.
Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.
Testing How Often Wall Squats Are Needed
To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.
Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.
To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.
Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.
The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.
After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.
Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.
Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits
After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.
These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.
By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.
The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.
By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.
Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.
Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade
The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.
Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.
This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.
However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.
"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.
"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."
Story Source:
Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Harry T Swift, Charles Pedlar, Damian A Coleman, John P Buckley, Jonathan D Wiles. Isometric exercise training and blood pressure control: exploring the dose-response to training frequency in a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open Sport, 2026; 12 (3): e003172 DOI: 10.1136/bmjsem-2025-003172

articles.title: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
articles.text:
Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?
Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.
In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.
RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.
This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.
The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).
At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.
Is self-improving AI 'nonsense'?
Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.
In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).
Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.
Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.
"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.
Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.
The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.
"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.
The challenge of true RSI
The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment
- Google DeepMind's latest AI tool promises a new era for genetics research, but experts warn to take its predictions with caution
- OpenAI claims we've entered the AGI era — has GPT-6 Astra really demonstrated general intelligence?
Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.
Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.
She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

Owen Hughes is a freelance writer and editor specializing in data and digital technologies. Previously a senior editor at ZDNET, Owen has been writing about tech for more than a decade, during which time he has covered everything from AI, cybersecurity and supercomputers to programming languages and public sector IT. Owen is particularly interested in the intersection of technology, life and work – in his previous roles at ZDNET and TechRepublic, he wrote extensively about business leadership, digital transformation and the evolving dynamics of remote work.
