articles.title: Waymo taps Toyota to supply robotaxis for Japan and the UK | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Waymo will begin testing autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year as part of a broader partnership with the automaker to provide electric vehicles for robotaxi operations in international markets, including the U.K.
Under the partnership announced Friday, Toyota will manufacture the 2027 bZ4X vehicles and integrate Waymo’s self-driving system at its Takaoka factory in Japan. (The electric vehicle is now known as the bZ in the North American market.)
The autonomous bZ4X vehicles will initially be tested in Japan, where Waymo intends to eventually operate a robotaxi service. But the intent is to deploy these vehicles in other right-hand driving countries such as the U.K. Waymo has been testing its autonomous Jaguar I-Pace vehicles in London for months and plans to launch a robotaxi service there once it receives the necessary permits.
The announcement comes 18 months after Toyota and Waymo signed a preliminary agreement to explore the development and deployment of an autonomous vehicle platform. At the time, the agreement fell into the “let’s see what happens” category, with language vague enough to leave plenty of room for interpretation.
For now, the partnership looks more like a conventional vehicle supplier deal that helps Waymo fill specific regional needs while adding a new model to its robotaxi portfolio.
But the partnership could go beyond robotaxis. The companies said they will continue to look at bringing Waymo’s autonomous technology to personally owned Toyota vehicles.
Toyota and Waymo also announced plans to look at other future “initiatives” that would use “insights from Waymo’s real-world operations” to improve safety for other road users. What that might mean is unclear, although Hiroki Nakajima, executive vice president of Toyota and a board member, provided some clues.
“This collaboration will help scale that technology and bring it to customers in Japan and beyond through Waymo’s ride-hailing service, and in parallel, Toyota will continue to explore how integrating vehicles with traffic infrastructure can make those roads safer still,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
articles.text:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek Mulvey
But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

articles.title: Vizio’s discounted Mini LED TV lets you skip the sign-ups and smarts
articles.text:
Modern smart TVs let you skip the streaming device, which is convenient, but they also come with their own issues, including privacy concerns and frequent updates. The Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV lets you cut out the rigamarole and just get straight to the HDMI ports. And right now, it’s discounted at Walmart, with the 65-inch model going for $358 ($40 off) and the 85-inch model going for $698 ($100 off).
Vizio’s discounted Mini LED TV lets you skip the sign-ups and smarts
If you prefer a dedicated streaming device or console, you can save some cash on an otherwise-modern television.
Although Vizio’s Mini LED TV comes loaded with Vizio OS, you can bypass the TV’s host of agreements during setup. By pushing past the manufacturer’s warnings about “missing out” on smart TV features, you can disable the built-in operating system, letting you use your own streaming device like a Roku or Apple TV 4K without worrying about what data Vizio and Walmart might be collecting.
As for specs, the TV features quantum dots for full, vivid color and high brightness (our testing showed it can reach 936 nits when calibrated thanks to its mini-LED panel). There are some compromises, though, which is expected given the low price point. The IPS panel doesn’t have the best black levels, as you might see on more expensive sets, and there’s a touch of motion blur during faster scenes, which may also hurt its appeal for gamers. It also has three HDMI ports, but they’re only 2.0, although the screen only supports up to 4K at 60Hz, so it’s not detrimental to the experience.

articles.title: Thrive Holdings agrees to buy ADT for $7.6bn, financed by Apollo
articles.text:
Thrive Holdings, the holding company set up by Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, has agreed to buy ADT for $10 a share in cash. ADT sells home security systems in the US. The deal values ADT at about $7.6bn in equity and $15.3bn in enterprise value.
The price is a 45.6% premium to ADT’s close of $6.87 on 27 October, the companies said in a joint announcement on Thursday. ADT’s board approved it unanimously. ADT shares rose 34% on the news, The Information reported.
“ADT is pleased to enter into this transaction, which recognizes the value built by our more than 12,000 employees and delivers an attractive cash premium to our stockholders,” said Jim DeVries, ADT’s chairman and chief executive.
Apollo returns as the lender
Funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management are providing all of the financing. Apollo is ADT’s former owner, Claire Rychlewski reported for Axios. It took ADT private in 2016 and brought it back to the New York Stock Exchange in 2018. It sold its remaining stake five months ago.
The deal needs approval from ADT’s shareholders and US antitrust regulators. The companies expect it to close in the first quarter of 2027. Until 28 November, ADT may look for better offers, with a possible 10-day extension for some bidders. Once the sale closes, ADT’s shares will stop trading.
A holding company with OpenAI behind it
Thrive Capital set up Thrive Holdings last year as a permanent capital vehicle. That lets it own businesses for longer than a typical private equity firm. It owns more than 75 businesses in accounting, IT services and the built environment. ADT will become the base of its smart home security business.
OpenAI is a partner and an investor in Thrive Holdings, according to TechCrunch. It supplies AI models and engineers to the companies Thrive owns. Thrive Capital has also disclosed a $215m Amazon stake. Joshua Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Thrive said in a blog post that new technology could cut false alarms and make alerts more informative. It could also spot faulty equipment earlier. Neither company has announced new products.
Customer data
ADT’s data and privacy policies will stay the same, the companies said. No new data sharing will happen without customers’ permission.
“Protecting customers’ homes also means protecting their data,” said Anuj Mehndiratta, a partner at Thrive Holdings.
ADT technicians sell and install Google Nest devices and Apple’s new smart home range, The Verge reported. Apple launched that range, including its $299 HomeView hub, this month. Amazon put a camera in its new Echo Studio this week.
ADT will report its third-quarter results on 3 November and will not take questions on the call.

articles.title: Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is $60 off just in time for sweater weather
articles.text:
As the weather cools, it may be worth investing in a smart thermostat to help lower your energy bills. Right now, Google’s fourth-gen Nest Learning Thermostat is on sale in all three colors for $219.99 ($60 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and The Home Depot, matching its best price of the year and just $10 shy of its all-time low.
Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is $60 off just in time for sweater weather

Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is its most capable to date, and comes with new features designed to lower energy consumption without sacrificing comfort. Like prior models, it learns your heating and cooling preferences over time and automatically creates a schedule based on your habits, so you don’t have to constantly adjust the temperature yourself. It can also suggest schedule changes to save energy and automatically adjusts the temperature when you’re away. Additionally, it includes a remote temperature sensor in the box, so you can better adjust the temperature in your preferred room, whether that’s the bedroom or another space in your home.
The Nest Learning Thermostat also improves on its predecessor with a beautifully designed adaptive display that shows your temperature settings, the weather, and the time from across the room. When you get closer, it reveals more detailed information, including outdoor air quality and humidity levels. The Matter-ready device also works with more HVAC systems than the third-gen model, along with a host of compatible humidifiers, dehumidifiers, and ventilation equipment. Plus, unlike many smart thermostats, it doesn’t require a C-wire in most homes either, though using one can help ensure consistent power.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says it's time to look beyond tech. Here are 4 consumer stocks he likes
articles.text:
Investors looking to diversify beyond the struggling artificial intelligence trade should consider consumer staples stocks, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Friday.
The Nasdaq-100, which tracks the biggest tech stocks, ended October down almost 7%. Investors rotated into other more defensive areas of the market. The S&P 500 Equal Weight gained roughly 5% for the month. (The equal weight index treats all the S&P 500 stocks the same, rather than weighting them by market cap.) The consumer staples index surged 11.4%, making it the second-best performing sector behind energy.
"You've got to take what the market is giving you, and until we sort out some of the issues for the tech sector, some other groups might be better bets for the time being," the "Mad Money" host said. "I like the idea of camping out in the staples for a bit."
Cramer highlighted four companies he finds particularly attractive in consumer staples — a group that features companies with household brand names that people tend to buy regardless of market conditions or economic environment.
- Kimberly-Clark: The maker of Kleenex tissues and Huggies diapers is one of the newest holdings in Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club. Cramer sees significant upside from its pending merger with Kenvue, which owns brands including Tylenol and Band-Aid. He expects the deal to generate efficiencies and create a consumer products powerhouse. Kimberly-Clark shares gained nearly 11% in October, but the stock still trades at less than 15 times earnings, with a 4.7% dividend yield. "I think the move is just getting started," Cramer said.
- Procter & Gamble: While the Investing Club exited its longtime P&G position in July, Cramer said the company remains an attractive defensive investment following better-than-expected quarterly results last week. He also expressed confidence in new CEO Shailesh Jejurikar. Shares of Procter & Gamble rallied 11% in October, though Cramer prefers Kimberly-Clark's lower valuation and higher dividend yield.
- Constellation Brands: The maker of Modelo and Pacifico beers is showing signs of a turnaround, with its core beer business gaining market share and its smaller wine and spirits division reporting 15% shipment growth last quarter. Shares of Constellation Brands surged 20% in October, but Cramer still sees value in the stock, which trades at roughly 11 times earnings and yields more than 3%. "It increasingly looks like the worst is behind Constellation Brands," Cramer said.
- Coca-Cola: This is the one Cramer favors among the major soda makers. Coca-Cola delivered a strong quarterly report on Tuesday driven by higher volume rather than price increases. He also praised its innovation in zero-calorie beverages and its protein options with its Fairlife milk business. Shares gained 9% in October.

articles.title: Cramer’s week ahead: Expect more volatility as tech earnings, midterms loom
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over.
Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. The S&P 500 followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%.
"After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the "Mad Money" host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings."
"My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher."
With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.
Monday
Apple reports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said.
Cramer also expects encouraging results from Palantir when it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software.
Tuesday
The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them."
On the earnings front, Advanced Micro Devices reports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector following Intel's disappointing results. Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel.
Drugmakers Pfizer and Amgen also report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks.
Wednesday
CVS Health reports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said.
McDonald's earnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees.
Thursday
Kimberly-Clark reports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger with Kenvue. The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said.
Friday
The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields.
The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners.

articles.title: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
articles.text:
Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.
The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.
Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."
A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.
"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."
Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.
The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.
S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

articles.title: Beware these stock funds for big capital gains distributions this year. How to manage the tax bill
articles.text: A year-end surprise is coming for mutual fund investors: Actively managed funds are poised to distribute capital gains, some of them enormous, to shareholders. October volatility notwithstanding, the S & P 500 is heading for its fourth consecutive year of double-digit gains; it's up more than 10% year to date. "We've seen some strong gains in the market, specifically around the artificial intelligence trade," said Morningstar senior manager research analyst Stephen Welch. He recently compiled the firm's list of funds with the highest estimated distributions for 2026. "We had strong markets in the past several years, so mostly these funds are sitting on unrealized capital gains," Welch added. Fund families are rolling out estimates for their capital gains distributions, which will transfer to shareholders in December. The distributions could be hefty, depending on several factors. Consider the Nationwide Renaissance Small Cap Growth Fund (NWGPX) , which is heading for an estimated distribution of 56.6% of its net asset value. The A-share version of the MFS Global Equity Fund (MWEFX) is set for a distribution in a range of 31% to 33% of NAV. The culprit Capital gains distributions can be unexpected for investors, who are left on the the hook for taxes even if they don't sell any shares. "I think of it as the Christmas surprise, between Thanksgiving and Christmas, if you're not paying attention to it, you get this big long-term capital gain, and if your planner isn't paying attention to it, it can throw a wrench into your tax projections," said Brian Kearns, founder of Haddam Road Tax & Consulting in Evanston, Illinois. Affected investors are holding these funds in their taxable brokerage accounts. The IRS deems the distributions to be long-term capital gains, regardless of how long an investor has held the fund. That means the distribution is subject to a rate of 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on your taxable income. You won't be affected if you hold the fund in a tax-deferred account, like an individual retirement account or a 401(k). Funds push out capital gains for several reasons. First, if a fund experiences significant outflows, the fund manager needs to sell appreciated securities to cash out departing shareholders. "This has been another year of a similar story of flows coming out of traditional mutual funds and going to ETFs, more passive-oriented options," said Welch. Strong performances in technology and emerging markets have also resulted in significant returns for those funds, he added, another driver of big distributions. Finally, one-off manager changes or updates to investment strategies can result in major distributions, Welch said. The tax bill The good news about the heads up on the distribution is that investors still have some time to prepare for it. For starters, tax-loss harvesting involves selling losing holdings and using those realized losses to offset capital gains elsewhere in the portfolio. If losses exceed capital gains, you can apply up to $3,000 of the loss against ordinary income. Any unused loss can be carried forward into future years. Resist selling funds that have a habit of churning out capital gains distributions: You'll end up on the hook for the appreciation you've had since you've held the fund. "If you've owned the fund for five, 10, 15 years, you might be sitting on a large gain yourself," said Jeff DeMaso, editor and founder of The Independent Vanguard Adviser. "You wouldn't sell a position you're up 100% in to offset your capital gains." Have your capital gains distributions go to cash, rather than having them reinvested into the fund, he said. "You can use the distribution to help rebalance the portfolio. You can also start directing some cash to maybe a more tax-friendly fund, an index fund or an ETF." "You'll still have your existing shares and you might face more capital gains distributions next year, but it starts to nudge the portfolio to a more tax-friendly stance," said DeMaso.

articles.title: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
articles.text:
A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens.
Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.
Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company. The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach.
The company says it will cover customers' losses. Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds.
For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back.
What happens to your crypto when an exchange gets hacked
Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026.
But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses.
In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed.
Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024.
"When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it."
What you should look for when choosing a crypto exchange
When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated.
U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database. Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company.
Crypto experts also recommend reading an exchange's user agreement or terms of service. Some exchanges might have separate custody agreements or risk disclosures that are worth checking, too, Mulyadi says.
Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk.
In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers.
"If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says.
Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.
Is it safer to keep your crypto on an exchange or hold it yourself?
If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody."
With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it.
That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe.
And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says.
For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them.
"Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says.

articles.title: Reddit stock plunges 29% after weak outlook, wrapping its worst day ever
articles.text:
Shares of Reddit cratered 29.22% on Friday, the worst drop since becoming a public company in 2024, after the company forecast weak fourth-quarter sales in its latest earnings report.
The previous record low was set on July 31, when the stock dropped 20.99%.
The social media company on Thursday projected fourth-quarter sales between $1 billion and $1.03 billion, below analysts' estimates of $1.05 billion. Reddit reported Q3 sales growth of 53% over a year ago, weaker than previous quarters, but beat Wall Street expectations on both earnings and revenue.
The report comes as the company has seen a shift in its search referral traffic with the rise of Google's AI Overview. In an interview with CNBC, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to AI.
Reddit announced on Thursday that it plans to test requiring users to log in to access content, a dramatic change from a site whose community-based discussion content has become synonymous with the open internet. Google's shift towards pushing AI overviews in search results coincided with the change, intended to help boost the number of logged-in users that are more active on the platform, which in turn helps the company's advertising business, according to Huffman.
"Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me. I've been holding that line," Huffman said. "I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work."
Multiple analysts downgraded the stock following Reddit's disappointing results, with Citizens noting that "search changes highlight the problem with selling content to Google" and that as referral problems worsen, uncertainty around user growth amid the login requirement switch "puts more pressure on user monetization."
— CNBC's Jonathan Vanian contributed to this report.

articles.title: Midterms, Apple earnings, jobs report. Wall Street faces a big week ahead just as investors dump tech
articles.text: The U.S. midterm elections are finally here, but investors suspect it will matter little to a market that's preoccupied with rumblings in the artificial intelligence trade. Early polling and prediction markets data suggest Democrats have a shot at winning majorities in both the House and the Senate. Such an outcome could have wide-ranging implications for government policy, including a potential unwind in defense spending — and maybe greater pricing pressures on pharmaceutical companies. More importantly, it could shape regulation around data centers, which could be consequential for tech companies. But investors are not too worried that Tuesday's vote will do much to move the market, which remains pinned to the AI trade and incoming earnings. "There's going to be volatility," said Mark Malek, investment chief at Siebert Financial. "But I think at the end of the day, there's just so many other macro themes that are so much more important right now." The major averages posted a losing week on Friday, with tech stocks leading a sell-off following disappointing results from Amazon and Intel . Google-parent Alphabet also plunged 12% on Thursday, its worst one-day decline on record, and dropped another 1.7% on Friday. .SPX 5D mountain SPX 5-day chart The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell 2.4% for the week, after enjoying a brief resurgence at the start of the week. It tumbled 9.1% on Friday. Most of the 11 S & P 500 sectors notched weekly gains, however, as traders ducked for cover in things like health care and consumer staples. Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble were notable outperformers. Amazon was the third hyperscaler after Alphabet and Meta Platforms to report negative free cash flow. That compounded investor worries that the rising debt of the biggest tech companies could signal broader financial stress among smaller companies while financial conditions tighten. Following the news, BTIG chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky warned again that the S & P 500 is vulnerable to a sell-off. He thinks the index will soon test its 200-day moving average, at 7,306, which represents a more than 5% slide from where it closed Thursday. That worry will loom over investors, as they watch for incoming earnings results. There are 138 S & P 500 companies set to report next week. That includes Apple and other major AI companies such as Palantir Technologies . The third-quarter earnings season has proven to be strong, but that's not thanks to the "Magnificent Seven" — which has hardly been magnificent of late . The S & P 500 is still projected to post earnings growth of about 30% for the third quarter, per FactSet. However, companies on average are only beating earnings expectations by 1.4%, far lower than both the five- and 10-year averages of 7.5% and 8%, as of Thursday. That drop is almost entirely due to Meta Platforms' and Alphabet's disappointing reports, according to John Butters, senior earnings analyst at FactSet. Apple earnings Poor results from the hyperscalers raise the stakes for Apple, the Magnificent Seven stock that is breaking away from the pack. Not only is the iPhone maker the best performer of the group — shares are up 28% year to date — it's also zeroing in on Nvidia's market capitalization and could soon win back the title of the world's most valuable public company. Apple is also starting to prove how it can differentiate itself in an era of greater AI adoption, as its buzzy new iPhone Duo that hit stores Oct. 23 could help the tech company revive its flagging hardware business. On Friday, however, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan warned there could be trouble on the horizon for Apple as well, with the bank removing the stock from its US1 list of best investment ideas. Mohan wrote that he has a "more conservative outlook" than the Street, given the potential impact that a staggered launch of iPhones could have on gross margins. 'Things that go bump in the night' There are other hurdles for the market ahead, including the October jobs report. While on the surface the labor market has continued to exhibit strength, there are widening chasms beneath that are worrisome for a consumer already beset with higher prices. The U.S. is expected to have added 55,000 jobs in October, with the unemployment rate holding steady at 4.2%, per FactSet. That would be an improvement from the prior month when the employment picture worsened to just 29,000 nonfarm payrolls. Other macroeconomic threats in the form of higher interest rates and yields, greater inflation and oil prices, continue to persist. But many investors remain constructive on the market. Part of that has to do with the historical pattern. In data going back to 1934, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 2.8% in the eight trading days surrounding midterm election days, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. And seasonally speaking, traders are headed into the best six months on the calendar for the stock market. November is the No. 1 month for the Nasdaq during midterm election years, with the tech-heavy index rising 3.5% on average, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. It's the second best month for both the Dow and the S & P 500 in midterm election years; the indexes average monthly gains of 2.6% and 2.7%, respectively. "If you had to say today, 'Mark, are you buying or selling?' I'm buying," Malek said, adding: "But just also increasing my inventory of things that go bump in the night." articles.title: Tech gets crushed, defensive stocks shine. How we're making sense of it all
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are sharply lower on the last trading day of a rough month of October, with tech stocks under severe pressure as the market continues to push back on AI-related names. The S & P 500 is down more than 2% on Friday, while the Nasdaq is down over 3.5%. Gains on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday seem like a distant memory against back-to-back days of selling. Amazon , Alphabet , and Microsoft fell over the past few days, and each stock was lower in the sessions after their earnings. The declines in Amazon and Microsoft were less warranted as Amazon CEO Andy Jassy outlined a bullish multiyear outlook for Amazon Web Services, with operating margins at their highest in company history — and Microsoft showed that Azure cloud revenue growth continued to accelerate even as the company didn't spend all its cash flow on AI infrastructure. But the market's reaction suggests investors' appetite is waning for the increasingly capital-intensive part of the AI buildout. Jim Cramer said Friday morning that the Amazon dip is buyable . Amazon already has our 1 rating. We're also getting closer to upgrading Microsoft to a buy-equivalent 1 if its slide continues. We're keeping our hold-equivalent 2 rating on Alphabet until its price-to-earnings multiple becomes too cheap to ignore and management acknowledges the weakness in Gemini and Search. Semiconductors are getting hammered after Intel gave a disappointing outlook that we covered Thursday night and on Friday's Morning Meeting . Intel is down over 30% on Friday. The data center story at Intel is still mostly intact, but what we got wrong was the sharp drop in personal computer CPU demand due to the high cost of memory and some execution hiccups. To make matters worse, Sandisk failed to impress with earnings Thursday evening, sending that stock down 15% on Friday. The last few days have been a win for diversification — keeping powder dry and owning several non-AI stocks that may not have the same revenue and earnings upside as faster-growing tech names but are far more predictable with their results and cash flow. All three of our healthcare stocks outperformed this week, led by Eli Lilly after a strong beat and raise quarter. Lilly shares surged to another all-time high Friday. Gains in those names have provided some relief from sharp losses in Intel, Alphabet, Salesforce, and Boeing. We still want to add more shares to our Boeing position. It's another big week of earnings ahead , with over 100 companies in the S & P 500 scheduled to report. Within the portfolio, It's Apple on Monday evening, DuPont and Eaton on Tuesday morning, Qnity Electronics before Wednesday's open, and Cardinal Health and Kimberly-Clark on Thursday morning. Other notable names scheduled are Advanced Micro Devices, Palantir, Amgen, McDonald's, Qualcomm, Uber, Affirm, CVS Health, Wynn Resorts, and Pfizer. It's also a busy week of economic data , with ISM manufacturing and services reports, durable goods and factor orders — and, of course, the October nonfarm payrolls report on the docket. Economists polled by FactSet expect a gain of 72,500 jobs in October, with a 0.3% month-over-month increase in average hourly earnings, and an unemployment rate unchanged from 4.2% in September. The midterms are Tuesday . They have been a key date on our radar. Our focus is less on the election results and more on what happens afterward. We want to see whether the elections lead to an easing of anti-data center rhetoric and greater clarity on how the Trump administration plans to approach the conflict in the Middle East. articles.title: UnitedHealth is finally getting its act together. I'm buying into the turnaround
articles.text: Part of my investment process is finding strong management teams that have a successful track record. UnitedHealth Group fits the bill. The Eden Prairie, Minnesota-based company is one of the world's largest health insurers, providing coverage to individuals, employers and Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries through its UnitedHealthcare business. It also operates Optum, which spans direct patient care and health care technology. Key points A diversified business model that provides revenue streams beyond traditional health insurance. Investments in AI and technology could improve efficiency and create new opportunities for growth. We're starting to see progress in controlling medical costs and strong earnings outlook. UnitedHealth ran into trouble last year as rising medical costs squeezed profits. In May 2025, the company withdrew its earnings guidance, sending shares down 17.4% that day. Then Stephen Hemsley returned as CEO. He previously ran the company from 2006 to 2017, a period during which the stock appreciated roughly 354%. So I think it's fair to say he did a pretty good job the first time around. Shortly after returning, Hemsley also personally purchased $25 million worth of UnitedHealth stock. That's an endorsement if I've ever seen one. Now UnitedHealth has delivered better-than-expected earnings in recent quarters and raised its full-year guidance. That's a strong sign that the company is getting back on track. Why I'm buying More than just an insurance company Through Optum, the company has built a diversified healthcare services business that includes Optum Health, Optum Rx and Optum Insight. These businesses provide direct patient care, manage prescription drug benefits, and offer technology and data analytics services. So UnitedHealth gets additional sources of revenue beyond traditional insurance premiums, including recurring service fees and opportunities for higher margins. The scale is enormous. In the third quarter, Optum generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings, compared with $86.3 billion in revenue and $2.8 billion in operating earnings at UnitedHealthcare. Betting big on AI and technology UnitedHealth plans to invest nearly $1.5 billion in technology initiatives in 2026 alone, including artificial intelligence. The goal is to automate workflows and reduce the time it takes to process prior authorizations and approvals. These might not sound like the most exciting applications of AI, but I think they could make a real difference for a company of UnitedHealth's size. When you're serving tens of millions of people, even relatively small improvements in efficiency can add up. In addition to cutting costs, this could also improve the experience for patients and healthcare providers while creating additional opportunities for Optum's technology business. Getting medical costs under control Rising medical costs were a big reason the company ran into trouble in the first place. But Hemsley has been addressing that through a broad effort to streamline the business and adjust its portfolio. A key measure I'm watching is the medical care ratio, which tells us how much of the company's insurance premium revenue goes toward paying for medical services. The lower that ratio, the more room the insurer has to make a profit. UNH YTD mountain UnitedHealth Group Incorporated, YTD In the third quarter, UnitedHealth's medical care ratio fell to 88.4%, down from 89.9% a year earlier and better than analysts expected. The company also reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share , beating expectations, and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share. Why now? We're still in the early stages of a turnaround, but there are several reasons to be optimistic about what comes next. For one, the company stands to benefit from an aging population. Roughly 10,000 baby boomers are reaching traditional retirement age each day, creating continued demand for Medicare coverage and healthcare services. I'm also encouraged by the company's longer-term earnings growth ambitions. Management is targeting annual earnings growth of 13% to 16%. The stock has already staged an impressive recovery, climbing about 27% year to date. Shares are now just 11% below their 52-week high, but I believe there's still room for the turnaround to play out. Bottom line Medical costs remain a risk. If utilization rises faster than expected or the company's efforts to improve profitability take longer to materialize, that could put pressure on earnings. But Hemsley has successfully led this company before. I believe he can do it again. For me, this is an opportunity to own a leading health care company with a proven leader at the helm, at a valuation that remains below its historical average. Stephanie Link is the Chief Investment Strategist at Hightower Advisors, where her division manages $8.5 billion in assets (as of June 4, 2026). She has 35 years of experience managing money and serves on KKR's investment council. She earned a B.S. in finance from Boston College. Disclosures: Link owns in Hightower Advisors. articles.title: Reid Hoffman gives millions to Dems in late spending spree as Epstein fight spills into election
articles.text:
Billionaire venture capitalist Reid Hoffman has put $8 million into the Democratic Party of Wisconsin over the past five weeks to help the party's gubernatorial nominee David Crowley in his race against Republican Tom Tiffany.
The LinkedIn co-founder gave $2 million on Sept. 24, $1 million on Oct. 2 and another $5 million in two installments on Oct. 5 and Oct. 20, according to Wisconsin campaign finance records. The rapid-fire checks are part of a last-minute spending spree by some of America's richest donors before Election Day.
In just the past week and a half, former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg gave Democratic Texas gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa $750,000, while Y Combinator co-founder Jessica Livingston chipped in another $150,000, state records show.
Bloomberg had already committed roughly $80 million to help Democrats this fall, much of it aimed at winning control of the House.
Meanwhile, PayPal co-founder Luke Nosek gave $500,000 on Tuesday to Judicial Fairness PAC, which supports conservative judicial candidates in Texas, according to Texas campaign finance records. The group had already received $2 million from Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, according to state records. Musk's roughly $475 million in disclosed political giving through late October makes him the cycle's biggest known individual donor.
The checks are landing in the middle of a final-week ad frenzy, with more than $1 billion now booked to air before Election Day, according to AdImpact. The 2026 cycle has already broken the record for political ad spending, with more than $11.2 billion spent or reserved, according to AdImpact. That's more than any previous presidential election cycle as well.
Hoffman has framed his own spending as a reluctant necessity.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote Friday on X. "And while others spend outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."
The House Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect House Democrats, has received $8.5 million from Hoffman this cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records.
In the past two weeks, the group has rolled out 13 ads related to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. They total about $8.4 million in spending and nearly 719.4 million impressions, according to AdImpact. Until this month, it had not run a single Epstein-focused ad.
The spots have pushed Epstein into at least six battleground House races, accusing Republicans of helping block the release of government records related to Epstein or highlighting their ties to people in his orbit.
In Arizona's Second District, an ad called "Justice" attacked Republican Rep. Eli Crane over votes related to releasing the Epstein files and contributions from alleged Epstein associates. In Pennsylvania's Eighth District, ads called "Predators" and "Teacher" targeted Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan. And this week, an ad called "Exposed" went after Republican Rep. Mike Turner in Ohio's Tenth District over a contribution from an Epstein confidant and his record on releasing the files. All three races are tightly contested and could help determine control of the House in the next Congress.
There is no way to trace Hoffman's money to any particular ad because super PACs pool contributions from their donors. But the blitz comes with an obvious complication for Democrats: Hoffman's continued association with Epstein after the financier pleaded guilty in 2008 to sex offenses involving a minor.
Hoffman has acknowledged visiting Epstein's private island and meeting with him after the conviction. He has said the relationship grew out of fundraising for the MIT Media Lab and has repeatedly said he regrets continuing to meet with Epstein.
"My last interaction with Epstein was in 2015," Hoffman told Axios in 2019. "Still, by agreeing to participate in any fundraising activity where Epstein was present, I helped to repair his reputation and perpetuate injustice. For this, I am deeply regretful."
There is no allegation that Hoffman participated in Epstein's sex-trafficking crimes, but Republicans have nevertheless seized on the relationship. The Republican National Committee this week accused Democrats of hypocrisy for accepting Hoffman's money while using Epstein against GOP candidates.
"Democrats have no problem with money in politics so long as it benefits their own campaign," RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Fox News earlier this week.
And the attack has followed Hoffman's money into Wisconsin. In a new 15-second ad, Tiffany's campaign splices together clips of Crowley saying "Epstein" and "billionaires" before a narrator says they "are bankrolling David Crowley's campaign."

articles.title: Binance hack: Investigators in a 'cat and mouse game' to recover $6.3 billion in stolen funds
articles.text:
Crypto firms and law enforcement are racing to recover more than $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance before hackers manage to hide the funds.
The firms say they're in a "cat and mouse game" against alleged North Korean hackers who are using a combination of crypto obfuscation techniques and professional global money laundering networks to turn their digital coins into fiat currency, according to experts who spoke to CNBC.
These moves underscore how hard it can be to recover the stolen funds after a crypto hack.
"Ultimately, they're [hackers] trying to off-ramp it [crypto] to fiat. And that becomes the challenge, that's sort of this race against time," Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, one of the companies investigating the Binance hack, told CNBC on Friday.
Binance pledged to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users.
Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis have attributed the Binance hack to a North Korean state-backed hacking group called TraderTraitor, which has a history of crypto cyberattacks.
Frozen stablecoins
After the hack, several stablecoin issuers, including Circle, which issues USDC, and Tether, which issues USDT, moved to freeze the funds. Stablecoins are digital coins that represent a currency, such as the dollar, 1-to-1 and are backed by assets such as government bonds or fiat.
Binance estimates that around $3 billion worth of cryptocurrency has been frozen so far.
The issuers of the stablecoins could burn and reissue the tokens and potentially recover those losses. In this scenario, a company like Circle or Tether would effectively destroy the frozen stablecoins, making them inaccessible to hackers. They could reissue new stablecoins that could be held in a legal government entity and then given back to Binance.
The hackers were one step ahead. They quickly moved to sell USDT to market makers and borrow the cryptocurrency ether against the stablecoin, according to TRM Labs. Ether is harder to freeze, and the entity the hackers borrowed from would be left with the stolen stablecoin.
"The attackers knew that route would be closed to them and so got out ahead of that," said Joe Hancock, a partner and head of cyber risk and complex investigations at law firm Mishcon de Reya.
Obfuscating stolen funds
Hackers have used sophisticated tactics to evade law enforcement and keep authorities from seizing the roughly $3 billion that remains.
Cryptocurrencies run on blockchains, which are public ledgers of transactions. That means crypto forensic firms can track the movement of crypto across different online wallets. So hackers use various techniques to throw investigators off their trail.
Crypto mixer services obscure the trail of cryptocurrency by mixing funds from different users, making it harder to track the money.
Jonathan Levin, CEO of Chainalysis, told CNBC there are no signs of this happening yet.
Instead, his company observed "laundering patterns we have not seen before," with hackers using automation to send funds back and forth between different wallets to throw investigators off their scent.
"Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence," Chainalysis wrote in a blog post.
If hackers swap stablecoins into cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum, it's not possible to freeze the assets.
Levin told CNBC that the hackers moved a lot of money to different Tron addresses. Tron is a blockchain.
"We've got teams working around the clock to continue to follow that," Levin said. "We also have automated mechanisms now to track that. It's not just manual work."
All of these tactics will make it harder for companies to track the stolen crypto, but TRM Labs' Redbord said his company is getting "better and better" at identifying these techniques.
"It's this continued cat and mouse game where bad actors are trying to obfuscate their transactions and we are trying to track and trace them," Redbord said.
Global money laundering networks
Hackers are increasingly using Chinese money laundering organizations to turn crypto into fiat, according to Chainalysis' Levin and TRM Labs' Redbord.
"So we are not necessarily only chasing North Korean on-chain, often we're chasing these professional money laundering networks," he said.
On-chain refers to transactions on blockchains, while off-chain refers to transactions not recorded there. That could be because it involves fiat currency.
Levin explained that money laundering organizations will offer to buy the stolen crypto over the counter for a large fee. They would then launder the money and get it back to the hackers, potentially in some form of stablecoin, which can then be exchanged for fiat currency.
When it gets to this stage, it becomes harder to recover stolen funds.
"As you get further and further away, the amount of seizure opportunities go down," Levin said.

articles.title: Why bitcoin held up better after the record Binance hack
articles.text:
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history, but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin, according to market analysts and researchers.
On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin. On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day.
By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital.
The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC.
"Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."
Binance hack isn't first to batter bitcoin
Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble.
In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data.
More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets.
What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options."
GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin.
"Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC.
The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day.
Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.
"Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment."

articles.title: Is it finally time to buy Lululemon? Here's what the charts tell me
articles.text: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) From its 2017 low to its 2023 high, Lululemon (LULU) surged nearly 1,000% before turning on a dime. As of its October low earlier this month, the stock had fallen 82% from its peak. Along the way, investors had plenty of chances to buy the dip, only to see the stock fall further. Even when LULU entered bear market territory or became oversold, the selling continued. Let's look at what hasn't worked and what it would take for LULU to establish a more lasting bottom. 1. Buying when a stock enters bear market territory LULU first declined 20% from its high in early 2024, officially entering bear market territory. That did nothing to stop the downtrend, which eventually extended beyond 80%. 2. Buying when a stock becomes oversold LULU's 14-week RSI first fell below 30 in April 2024. Again, this did little to stop the bleeding. Over the past two years, the indicator has largely oscillated between oversold territory and the midpoint of its range, a characteristic of a persistent downtrend. 3. A potential inverse head and shoulders pattern At CappThesis, we're always looking for bullish patterns, both in stocks making new highs and those attempting to bottom. Just a few days ago, we highlighted a potential inverse head and shoulders pattern that developed after LULU gapped considerably lower in September. A breakout could propel the stock into an area of relatively light overhead supply, potentially reaching a $119 measured-move target. Given the prolonged downtrend, we're managing risk with a $99 stop. Why this breakout needs to be different Over the past year, LULU has attempted to break out through five separate bullish patterns. Only one produced even a modest advance, which was quickly sold. This underscores the importance of seeing the latest breakout generate sustained upside rather than becoming another failed attempt. The bigger opportunity: Building a long-term base Small bullish patterns often provide tactical trading opportunities, but they can also establish the foundation for much larger formations. If LULU can sustain its breakout, reach $119 and eventually advance toward $130, a much larger basing pattern encompassing nearly six months of price action could emerge. That would provide a broader foundation for further upside and potentially position the stock to challenge its long-term downtrend. An 82% decline alone isn't a reason to buy What matters is whether LULU can finally demonstrate the technical characteristics of a sustainable bottom. The current pattern offers an initial opportunity with defined risk, and potentially the first step toward something much bigger. Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis , an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.
